The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

strengths: Soundness: The core construction in Eq. 3 is useful and largely correct: for a stochastic P and strictly positive ν, P_(ν) is stochastic, reversible with measure ν+P^Tν, and irreducible when the original digraph is weakly connected.

Evaluation and significance: The study spans ten K-NN graphs, three DiSBMs, two real directed networks, and ten baselines, with repeated runs and sensitivity analyses. ParPIC ties S-PIC at PRB 0.96 on K-NN graphs and performs especially well on the chain/core-periphery DiSBMs and PolBlogs.

Practicality: Avoiding eigendecomposition and using sparse power iterations plus random projections is potentially valuable for large directed-graph clustering. The ablations over γ, diffusion time, probe count, and embedding dimension are helpful.

Presentation: The pipeline, algorithm, tables, and appendices are organized and visually clear, and the manuscript generally distinguishes spectral, Hermitian, and power-iteration baselines. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-20va57ih/call-3ad488aa3bd8447c86d6ae012c54b77a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

Reproducibility and ethics: The authors provide code, dataset statistics, DiSBM probability matrices, baseline descriptions, run counts, and principal defaults. The benchmark-clustering setting raises no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive flaw: Proposition 3.5 is false. A reversible, irreducible, aperiodic transition matrix P=[[0.9,0.1],[0.8,0.2]] gives summed row entropy 0.8255 at t=1 but 0.7134 at t=2. It is realizable as P_(π) for a weighted undirected graph. The Jensen step is invalid because, for fixed j, the purported weights P(k,j) need not sum to one. Thus the claimed monotone entropy curve—and hence the theoretical basis for elbow selection—is unsupported.

The entropy definitions are internally inconsistent: Eq. 7 defines H as a sum, while the proof uses an average and states a limit missing a factor of N. Proposition 3.6's bound also relies on the false claim that each row entropy is bounded by the stationary entropy; a transient row can have greater entropy. Only unbiasedness and the finite-population variance identity survive as written.

The low-dimensional embedding does not approximate the paper's diffusion geometry. Eq. 4 weights coordinates by 1/π_(ν), whereas Z=P_(ν)^t Z0 preserves ordinary Euclidean distances between unweighted rows of P_(ν)^t. A stationary-measure rescaling is required, so the claimed link among the practical embedding, diffusion distance, and diffusion map is not established.

The method starts from P=D_out^{-1}W, which is undefined at sinks, yet PolBlogs and Email-Eu are explicitly said to contain many sinks. No dangling-node convention is specified. Likewise, strictly positive ν guarantees irreducibility under weak connectivity but does not guarantee aperiodicity, contrary to the prose.

The evidence does not justify several broad claims. There are only two real intrinsically directed networks; on Email-Eu, ParPIC (0.48±0.02) is slightly below S-PIC (0.49±0.01), and its PolBlogs result has high variability (0.39±0.14). The strongest gains are on tailored synthetic structures, with no significance testing or broader natural-network validation.

The scalability claim rests on one synthetic graph family and a runtime plot lacking hardware, implementation, preprocessing, selected-time, memory, and uncertainty details. No end-to-end complexity analysis includes the √N entropy probes, so improved scalability is not yet convincingly demonstrated.

Originality is moderate: the reversible operator is inherited from prior generalized-Laplacian work, while PIC and random projection are established. Moreover, P_(ν) has symmetric support and is equivalent to a random walk on an undirected weighted graph; it encodes directional information in weights but does not preserve non-reversible directional dynamics as repeatedly claimed.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: the manuscript omits the K used for K-NN graphs, feature preprocessing, sink handling, exact random-projection distribution/scaling, KNEEDLE settings and search horizon, seeds, eigensolver details, and runtime platform. It also lacks a candid limitations discussion covering known k, graph assumptions, parameter sensitivity, and limited real-network evidence.

strengths: Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, with a clear pipeline, explicit algorithm, readable tables, and a substantial appendix. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-l9wz2xll/call-8fb11200ce494dfcb7940b2f29689880/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Soundness of the operator construction: assuming a valid row-stochastic P and positive measure, Eq. 3 does yield a stochastic operator reversible with respect to ν+P^Tν; weak connectivity also gives irreducibility of its symmetrized support.

Significance: an eigen-free directed-graph clustering pipeline based on sparse power iterations and random projections could be practically useful, especially when dense decompositions are infeasible.

Evaluation breadth: the paper reports 100-run AMI results, multiple baseline families, synthetic and real graphs, and extensive sensitivity studies for γ, diffusion time, probe count, and embedding dimension. ParPIC is particularly strong on the designed chain and core-periphery DiSBMs.
Reproducibility and ethics: a code repository is linked, synthetic block matrices and many defaults are documented, and the generic clustering method presents no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. Its Jensen step treats P(k,j) as normalized over k, whereas row-stochasticity only gives Σ_j P(k,j)=1. For the reversible, irreducible, aperiodic chain P=[[0.9,0.1],[0.8,0.2]], the summed row entropy decreases from H(1)=0.8255 to H(2)=0.7134. This chain is also an undirected random walk and hence lies within the proposed class via P_(π)=P. Consequently, the theoretical basis of the entropy selector and the C(π)-based concentration bound in Proposition 3.6 are invalid.

There are additional entropy inconsistencies: Eq. 7 defines H as a sum over rows, while the proof alternates between a sum and an average and gives the limiting entropy of one row rather than N times that value. No result connects an entropy elbow—or its sampled estimate—to a clustering-optimal time.

Methodology: the defined diffusion distance weights coordinates by 1/π_(ν), but Algorithm 1 applies k-means to P_(ν)^tZ using an ordinary random projection, which approximates unweighted row distances. Thus the implemented embedding is not shown to preserve the paper's stated diffusion geometry; the suggested Gaussian or uniform projection is also given without a precise normalization or finite-dimensional guarantee.

Scope: P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet the paper emphasizes that PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks without specifying a dangling-node convention. Moreover, weak connectivity alone does not imply aperiodicity, although convergence of P_(ν)^t is used throughout. These omissions undermine both the advertised applicability and reproducibility.

Significance of the evidence is overstated. On K-NN graphs ParPIC only ties S-PIC in aggregate PRB (0.96). Among the two real directed networks, S-PIC slightly exceeds ParPIC on Email-Eu (0.49 versus 0.48), while the PolBlogs result is modest and variable (0.39±0.14). The largest gains occur on synthetic models designed around degree-heterogeneous directional flow, and no significance testing is reported.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported: Figure 3 uses one dense synthetic family and an unspecified classical spectral-clustering implementation, with no asymptotic analysis, memory measurements, hardware details, modern sparse eigensolver comparison, or large real graph. Both entropy estimation and embedding use √N probes/dimensions, costing roughly O(t|E|√N), so superiority over sparse k-eigenvector methods is not established.

Originality is moderate: the reversible measure-parametrized operator is attributed to Sevi et al. (2025), power-iteration clustering is established, and random projection plus knee detection are standard. The integration is useful, but its main new theoretical component is currently incorrect.

Reproducibility and limitations: important details are absent, including K-NN preprocessing and an explicit K, entropy search horizon and KNEEDLE settings, sink handling, seeds, software/hardware for timing, and some baseline fallback choices. Table 5 also lists 4000 DiSBM-CP vertices despite specifying 3×1300. The limitations discussion does not acknowledge these assumptions, the loss of antisymmetric flow under reversibilization, or the limited real-network advantage; the impact statement is boilerplate and could briefly discuss privacy-sensitive community inference on communication networks.

strengths: Significance: Directed-graph clustering without eigendecomposition is useful, and the combination of a measure-weighted reversible operator, sparse power iterations, random projection, and k-means forms a simple practical pipeline.

Empirical scope: Tables 2–3 compare ten baselines on ten k-NN graphs, three directed SBMs, and two real directed networks, reporting means and standard deviations over 100 runs. The appendices additionally vary degree heterogeneity, flow strength, cluster count, gamma, diffusion time, embedding dimension, and probe count. Results on the chain/core-periphery SBMs and PolBlogs are promising.

Presentation: The motivation, pipeline diagram, Algorithm 1, and main comparisons are generally clear. The paper also candidly reports that directionality provides little benefit on high-reciprocity k-NN graphs and that performance can depend substantially on gamma and diffusion time.

Reproducibility and ethics: Synthetic model matrices and several baseline formulas are provided, and a code repository is linked. This is a standard algorithmic study using existing datasets, with no apparent acute ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. Its Jensen step treats the column entries P(k,j) as normalized weights, although only rows of a stochastic matrix sum to one; reversibility does not make Shannon row entropy monotone. A direct counterexample satisfying the paper's assumptions is the reversible, aperiodic transition matrix [[0,1],[0.1,0.9]], obtainable as P_(pi) from the symmetric weighted graph [[0,1],[1,9]]. Its summed row entropy decreases from approximately 0.6276 at t=2 to 0.6074 at t=3. Moreover, because H(t) is defined as a sum over N rows, its limit is N times the entropy of pi, whereas Appendix E omits the factor N. Consequently, the theoretical basis for entropy-based time selection and the C(pi)-based bound in Proposition 3.6 is unsupported.

Soundness and claimed scope: The natural walk P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet the manuscript explicitly says PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks and never specifies a dangling-node convention. Treating sink rows as zero would also invalidate the stochasticity proof. In addition, positive nu and weak connectivity ensure neither aperiodicity nor convergence of P_(nu)^t; the proof only gives a self-loop condition, while the abstract and algorithm do not impose it or make the walk lazy.

Method–theory mismatch: Equation 4 defines diffusion distance using the stationary weighting 1/pi(k), but Algorithm 1 clusters unweighted rows of P_(nu)^t or a random projection preserving their ordinary Euclidean distances. Those distances are generally different; the implementation would need the corresponding stationary reweighting. Thus the diffusion-map property proved in Appendix E does not justify the actual embedding and clustering algorithm.

Evidence and significance: The strongest gains occur on three synthetic block models designed around asymmetric degree/flow patterns. There are only two small intrinsically directed real datasets (1,222 and 1,005 vertices); on Email-Eu, S-PIC slightly exceeds ParPIC (0.49 versus 0.48), while on the ten k-NN datasets ParPIC merely ties S-PIC in aggregate PRB (0.96). No significance tests are reported, and the broad claims of consistently outperforming alternatives and scaling to large graphs exceed this evidence. Figure 3 also omits hardware, repetitions, uncertainty, memory, and whether entropy-time selection is included.

Originality: The reversible operator is a random walk on the symmetric conductance matrix D_nu P + P^T D_nu and is closely tied to the cited generalized-Laplacian construction by overlapping authors; power iteration, Johnson–Lindenstrauss projection, and k-means are standard. The paper does not sharply separate its new contribution from that prior operator work, and its most distinctive component—the entropy rule—rests on the incorrect theorem. Claims that the reversible construction preserves directional dynamics should also be tempered: direction affects conductance weights, but the resulting support and dynamics are reversible and equivalent to an undirected weighted walk.

Reproducibility, presentation, and limitations: Important choices are absent or ambiguous, including sink handling, k-NN preprocessing and K, gamma values used for headline results, the maximum time/stopping rule and KNEEDLE configuration, projection distribution/scaling, k-means settings, random seeds, dataset provenance, and the DSC+ fallback's unspecified 'sufficiently large' time and starting row. Several appendix plots have very small labels, and the text inconsistently describes the numbers of datasets in Figures 9 and 10. The sensitivity discussion is useful, but there is no adequate limitations analysis of periodicity, dangling nodes, loss of nonreversible flow, or the potentially dense N-by-sqrt(N) entropy-probe computation; the impact statement is boilerplate and does not address data provenance or privacy implications of clustering social/email networks.

strengths: Significance: Directed-graph clustering without a full eigendecomposition is an important problem, and the proposed combination of reversible operators, power iteration, automatic time selection, and compressed embeddings is potentially useful.

Empirical breadth: The paper evaluates 10 K-NN datasets, three directed SBM settings, and two real directed networks against 10 baselines. The appendices include useful sensitivity studies over the vertex measure, diffusion time, embedding dimension, probe count, degree heterogeneity, flow strength, and number of clusters.

Experimental fairness: Giving all PIC variants the same entropy-based time selection and random projection helps isolate differences between their transition operators. Reporting averages and standard deviations over 100 runs is also valuable.

Presentation and reproducibility: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-v6df3pgg/call-944a99e8ae43449f9f1b806643c53740/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} is generally well organized, with an intuitive pipeline, readable pseudocode, extensive appendices, and a public code URL.

Originality: Although the ingredients are largely adaptations of prior work, assembling the parametrized reversible operator with a multi-vector PIC embedding and sampled entropy-based scale selection constitutes a discernible methodological contribution.

Ethics: This is primarily a methodological study using standard benchmark graphs, with no apparent acute safety or human-subject concern. The sensitivity analyses also honestly expose some parameter dependence.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive error: Proposition 3.5 is false. Reversibility does not imply that Shannon entropy increases under a Markov transition; this requires stronger conditions such as double stochasticity. For example, the reversible, aperiodic matrix P=[[0.9,0.1],[0.8,0.2]], which is itself a valid P_(ν) for an undirected weighted graph with ν equal to its stationary distribution, gives total row entropy H(1)=0.8255 and H(2)=0.7134. The proof misuses Jensen's inequality because the column entries P(k,j) do not generally sum to one. Consequently, the stationary-entropy bound used for Proposition 3.6 and its variance/confidence guarantees is unsupported, although unbiasedness of the sampling estimator remains valid.

Soundness: The implemented embedding does not realize the paper's defined diffusion geometry. Equation 4 weights row differences by 1/π_(ν)(k), whereas Equation 8 projects the unweighted rows of P_(ν)^t and Algorithm 1 clusters those projections. Standard JL projection therefore preserves a different distance. A factor such as D_{π}^{-1/2} would be needed; without it, the diffusion-map result in Appendix E does not justify the practical algorithm except in special cases such as uniform π.

Methodological claim: P_(ν) is a random walk on the symmetric conductance matrix B=D_νP+P^T D_ν. Thus every directed edge becomes bidirectional and non-reversible circulation is discarded. When γ=0, the construction is exactly the random walk on W+W^T, i.e. S-PIC; on in/out-regular digraphs it likewise collapses to ordinary symmetrization. The paper does not characterize precisely which directional information survives, so repeated claims that it preserves 'directional diffusion dynamics' are substantially overstated.

Domain of definition: The natural walk P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at zero-out-degree sinks, yet the paper emphasizes that PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks. No dangling-node convention or preprocessing is specified. Moreover, positive ν ensures irreducibility on weakly connected support but not aperiodicity; bipartite examples invalidate the claimed convergence of P_(ν)^t unless laziness or another assumption is added.

Evidence and significance: The strongest advantages are demonstrated on synthetic block models tailored to degree and flow asymmetry. On the two real directed networks, ParPIC obtains 0.39±0.14 on PolBlogs and 0.48±0.02 on Email-Eu, with S-PIC actually higher on Email-Eu at 0.49±0.01. On K-NN graphs it ties S-PIC in aggregate PRB and often trails it. Thus statements that ParPIC consistently outperforms all baselines are inaccurate, and evidence for broad real-world benefit is limited.

Scalability: No asymptotic analysis accompanies the central efficiency claim. With both projection dimension and entropy-probe count set to √N, sparse iterations cost approximately O(t|E|√N), which can be less favorable than computing k eigenvectors when k is small. Figure 3 covers one synthetic model and omits hardware, repetitions, memory, solver details, error bars, and strong sparse-eigensolver baselines, so it does not establish general scalability.

Originality: The reversible operator is closely inherited from the authors' prior generalized-Laplacian work, power-iteration clustering and random projection are established techniques, and KNEEDLE supplies the elbow detector. The main new theoretical component—the entropy criterion—is precisely where the central theorem fails, leaving the reliable novelty fairly incremental.

Reproducibility and presentation: Important operational details are missing, including the main-table value of γ, the K used for K-NN construction, feature normalization, dataset provenance and preprocessing, sink handling, the maximum time horizon and full KNEEDLE configuration, the reported random-projection distribution/scaling, random-seed protocol, and runtime environment. There are also mathematical inconsistencies: H is defined as a sum but treated as an average in its proof, its limiting constant misses the corresponding factor of N, and Section 2 writes an ordinary orthonormal eigendecomposition for a generally nonsymmetric random-walk matrix.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript has no substantive limitations section and does not acknowledge loss of circulation, dependence on known k, potentially sharp (γ,t) sensitivity visible in Figure 11, or the narrow real-network evaluation. The impact statement is boilerplate; clustering political and communication networks warrants at least brief discussion of privacy, profiling, and misuse risks.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for the ICML 2026 main research track.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance.

3 = Weak reject
There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly.

4 = Weak accept
The work is technically solid and advances an area in a useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

On K-NN graphs its aggregate PRB merely ties S-PIC. No paired significance tests or uncertainty for between-method differences are supplied.

The entropy elbow remains a heuristic independent of the requested cluster count k, with no recovery result connecting it to clustering quality. Figure 7 provides only descriptive evidence and includes cases such as Glass where the selected time is not best. KNEEDLE's search horizon and sensitivity/configuration are not reported, and the fixed-time descriptions are inconsistent.

The scalability claim lacks an asymptotic analysis and a reproducible timing protocol, including hardware, implementations, repetitions, and uncertainty. With both embedding dimension and entropy probes set to √N, the method can require O(t|E|√N) sparse work and O(N√N) dense storage, so it is not necessarily cheaper than computing k eigenvectors when k≪√N. Figure 3 uses only one synthetic model and one generic spectral comparator.

Originality and interpretation are overstated. P_(ν) is the random walk on the symmetric conductance D_νP+PᵀD_ν and builds directly on the cited Sevi et al. framework; multi-column random projection is a straightforward extension of PIC. The reversible construction retains some direction-dependent weights but necessarily removes non-reversible circulation. The paper does not characterize which directional information is preserved or identify non-identifiability/failure cases.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: the manuscript omits K-NN feature preprocessing and the explicit K value, dangling-node handling, projection normalization, k-means settings and seeds, exact main-table γ settings, baseline fallback details, and runtime environment. There are also internal presentation inconsistencies, such as mentioning PR-SC without reporting it and stating that Figure 9 covers four datasets when it shows seven.

Limitations are not treated adequately. The paper does not clearly discuss dependence on a known k, sensitivity to γ and t, potential negative/near-periodic modes, loss of directional circulation, or worst-case time and memory costs. The impact statement is boilerplate, although this is not itself a major ethical concern.

Overall, the useful operator construction and empirical signal do not compensate for a demonstrably false central proposition, an unresolved mismatch between the proposed geometry and implemented embedding, and an undefined treatment of sinks in the claimed application regime. Substantial theoretical correction and renewed evaluation are needed before acceptance.

strengths: The parametrized operator is simple and useful: for a strictly positive vertex measure, the manuscript correctly establishes stochasticity, reversibility with respect to ν+Pᵀν, and irreducibility on weakly connected support. The diffusion-distance spectral identity is also clearly derived.

The goal is significant: scalable clustering for weakly connected directed graphs without eigendecomposition is practically relevant. ParPIC gives a coherent pipeline combining a direction-aware operator, automatic time selection, random projection, and k-means.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, covering ten K-NN graphs, synthetic directed block models, and two real directed networks. The 100-run results, parameter-sensitivity studies, and controlled use of the same time-selection/projection machinery for all PIC variants are valuable.
The manuscript is well organized and visually polished, with readable algorithms, tables, figures, extensive appendices, and an available code repository. No acute ethical risk is apparent.
weaknesses: The decisive soundness problem is that Proposition 3.5 is false for general reversible Markov chains. Its Jensen step treats P(k,j) as normalized weights over k, although stochasticity only ensures normalization over j. Row entropy—and even its sum over rows—can decrease while a reversible, irreducible, aperiodic chain approaches a nonuniform stationary distribution. Consequently, the claimed monotonic basis for elbow selection and the C(π)-based bound in Proposition 3.6 are unsupported.

The entropy notation is internally inconsistent: Eq. 7 defines H as a sum, whereas the proof of Proposition 3.5 switches to an average and therefore states an incorrect limiting constant. Proposition 3.6 again uses the summed convention. Moreover, transient row entropy need not be bounded by the stationary entropy, invalidating its stated variance bound.

The implemented random projection Z=PᵗZ₀ preserves ordinary Euclidean distances between rows of Pᵗ, while the paper's parametrized diffusion distance weights coordinates by 1/π. Without projecting suitably rescaled rows, the practical embedding is not the diffusion-map geometry developed in Sec. 3.2, weakening the central interpretation.

The method begins with P=D_out⁻¹W but never specifies how zero-out-degree vertices are handled, despite explicitly emphasizing datasets with sinks. Likewise, a positive ν ensures irreducibility but not aperiodicity; the manuscript sometimes overstates that ν itself guarantees ergodicity.

Originality is moderate. The operator is the random walk on the symmetric conductance matrix DνP+PᵀDν and is substantially inherited from the cited Sevi et al. framework; PIC and random projection are established techniques. The claim that this reversible construction “preserves directional diffusion dynamics” needs a precise qualification because antisymmetric flow information is discarded.

The strongest gains occur on tailored, unusually dense synthetic block models. On the two real directed graphs, ParPIC improves on PolBlogs but is slightly worse than S-PIC on Email-Eu. This is insufficient to support broad superiority claims, especially without comparisons to directed SBM, flow/community-detection, or stronger scalable clustering baselines.

The scalability evidence is incomplete: Fig. 3 omits hardware, implementation details, uncertainty, and whether time-selection cost is included. With both embedding dimension and entropy probes set to √N, the sparse multiplication cost can scale as O(t|E|√N), so comparison against an unspecified “classical spectral clustering” implementation does not establish a general computational advantage.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: the manuscript omits explicit K-NN preprocessing and K, dangling-node treatment, main-table γ settings, KNEEDLE search range/settings, random seeds, k-means restart policy, and runtime environment. The printed Simple-Herm definition also uses W_ij in a case where W_ij=0, so the displayed matrix is not Hermitian as claimed.

The paper lacks a candid limitations discussion covering these failure conditions and the dependence on a supplied cluster count. Its impact statement is boilerplate and does not discuss data provenance or potential sensitivity when clustering political and email networks.

strengths: Methodologically, combining a vertex-measure-induced reversible walk with power-iteration clustering is coherent and practically motivated. The stochasticity, reversibility, and weak-connectivity-to-irreducibility parts of Proposition 3.2 are useful observations under their stated positivity and well-defined-transition assumptions.

The evaluation covers ten K-NN graphs, three directed SBMs, and two real directed networks, with ten baselines and repeated runs. The synthetic stress tests systematically vary flow strength, degree heterogeneity, cluster imbalance, and cluster count; ParPIC obtains strong results on the chain and core-periphery SBMs.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished. Algorithm 1, dataset statistics, baseline formulas, standard deviations, and extensive sensitivity plots make the approach easy to follow; a public code repository is also provided. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-egt9mwz_/call-780ccb7bff0a4b66af7f15494e623415/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The appendix honestly shows that γ and diffusion time can be dataset-sensitive and that directionality offers little benefit on highly reciprocal K-NN graphs. The work uses standard benchmarks and raises no immediate material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 3.5, which underpins the proposed time-selection method, is false. For the reversible, irreducible, aperiodic chain P=[[0.4,0.6],[0.1,0.9]], Eq. 7 gives H(1)=0.998 but H(2)=0.913. This chain can itself arise as P_(π) for an undirected weighted graph, so it satisfies the paper's setting. The proof misuses Jensen's inequality: P(k,j) does not sum to one over k merely because P is row-stochastic.

The same error propagates into Proposition 3.6. A transient row entropy need not be bounded by the stationary entropy C(π), invalidating the stated variance and concentration bounds, although unbiasedness of the sampling estimator remains correct. There is also a normalization inconsistency: Eq. 7 defines H as a sum over N rows, whose ergodic limit is N times the stationary entropy, whereas the proof gives only the single-row entropy.

The practical embedding is not the claimed diffusion embedding. Equation 4 uses the weighted distance ||(P^t_i-P^t_j)D_π^{-1/2}||, while Equation 8 randomly projects unweighted rows of P^t and therefore preserves, at best, ||P^t_i-P^t_j||. No stationary-distribution weighting or result connecting this surrogate to the stated diffusion geometry is supplied.

The advertised scope over weakly connected graphs is incomplete. P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet the manuscript explicitly emphasizes that PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain sinks and gives no dangling-node convention. Weak connectivity and positive ν also do not ensure aperiodicity; bipartite support remains periodic, undermining the convergence arguments used for entropy selection.

Significance and empirical support are overstated. Directional-network evidence contains only two modest-size real graphs, and most large gains occur on tailored synthetic SBMs without a model-matched directed-SBM inference baseline. On Email-Eu, S-PIC scores 0.49 versus ParPIC's 0.48, contradicting the claim that ParPIC outperforms all baselines.

The scalability claim lacks a complexity analysis. With d and the number of entropy probes both set to sqrt(N), repeated sparse multiplications can cost O(t|E|sqrt(N)), which is not automatically preferable to computing k eigenvectors using a sparse iterative solver. Figure 3 reports one unspecified spectral implementation without hardware, solver settings, repetitions, error bars, or clarification about whether time selection is included.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: the paper omits K-NN preprocessing and the value of K, sink handling, random-projection scaling and seeds, KNEEDLE parameters and search horizon, treatment of complex Hermitian embeddings, and runtime hardware. These omissions also make baseline fairness difficult to verify.

Originality is moderate: the reversible operator is substantially inherited from the cited generalized-Laplacian work, while PIC and random projection are established ingredients. The principal new entropy-selection component is empirically promising but rests on incorrect theory. Consequently, the central technical and evidential issues require more than a minor revision.

attempts.developer_message:
Please serve as an expert reviewer for the ICML 2026 main research track.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance.

3 = Weak reject
There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly.

4 = Weak accept
The work is technically solid and advances an area in a useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

strengths: Methodological idea: Equation (3) gives a simple measure-weighted reversibilization with an explicit stationary measure proportional to ν+Pᵀν, providing a usable operator for PIC-style clustering.

Practical significance: Randomized power iteration and sampled entropy estimation are straightforward and could be useful for moderately large graphs when the embedding dimension and probe count remain small.

Empirical effort: The paper evaluates 10 K-NN datasets, three directed block models, and two real directed networks against 10 baselines, reports variability, and includes sensitivity studies for γ, diffusion time, and embedding dimension.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is well structured, with an algorithm, notation table, dataset statistics, synthetic-model parameters, baseline descriptions, and a public code link. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-d28k5qk1/call-3c5a79b20cad474a8295a09ecddef04c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The discussion appropriately acknowledges that symmetrization is equally competitive on highly reciprocal K-NN graphs and that γ and diffusion time can be dataset-sensitive.
weaknesses: Soundness - decisive error: Proposition 3.5 is false as proved. Its Jensen step treats P(ν)(k,j) as convex weights over k, although row stochasticity only gives ∑j P(ν)(k,j)=1. A reversible, non-doubly-stochastic chain can have decreasing row entropy. The proof also changes H from the sum in Eq. (7) to an average and omits the resulting factor N in the limit. Consequently, the bound Hi(t)≤C(π(ν)) and the variance/concentration claims in Proposition 3.6 are unsupported; only unbiasedness is established. This undermines a central claimed contribution, automatic diffusion-time selection.

Soundness/applicability: P=Dout⁻¹W is undefined at sinks, yet the paper emphasizes that PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks and gives no dangling-node convention. Moreover, positive ν does not itself ensure aperiodicity, contrary to the prose following Proposition 3.2. Weakly connected graphs with bipartite undirected support can remain periodic, invalidating the convergence used by Proposition 3.5.

Method-objective mismatch: Eq. (4) uses the weighted norm ‖(Pt(i,·)-Pt(j,·))Dπ⁻¹/²‖, whereas Algorithm 1 and its random projection use PtZ without Dπ⁻¹/². The stated Johnson-Lindenstrauss argument therefore preserves ordinary row distances, not the manuscript's diffusion distance, particularly problematic on the degree-heterogeneous graphs motivating the method.

Originality and interpretation are overstated. P(ν) is exactly the random walk on the symmetric conductance matrix DνP+PᵀDν; for constant ν it reduces to an additive symmetrization and discards antisymmetric circulation. Thus it retains some direction-dependent weighting but does not generally preserve directed diffusion dynamics. The operator derives closely from the authors' prior generalized-Laplacian work, while PIC and random projection are standard.

The strongest gains are on dense synthetic chain/core-periphery models tailored around degree and flow asymmetries. There are only two intrinsically directed real datasets; ParPIC is not best on Email-Eu (0.48 versus 0.49 for S-PIC), and its PolBlogs result has high variability. On the 10 K-NN graphs it merely ties S-PIC in aggregate. These results do not support the broad claim of consistent superiority.

The evaluation objective is internally uneasy: the paper contrasts its density-based goal with flow-based methods, but its Chain and Core-Periphery models use cross-block probabilities up to 0.6 versus within-block probability 0.05, making their labels primarily flow/role clusters rather than density communities.

strengths: The P-RW construction is simple and computationally usable. Its reversibility and irreducibility under suitable positivity and connectivity assumptions are meaningful properties for diffusion methods on directed graphs.

The evaluation includes ten k-NN datasets, three directed SBMs, two real directed networks, ten baselines, repeated trials, and useful sensitivity analyses for the vertex measure, diffusion time, projection dimension, and entropy probes.

Applying the same projection and time-selection machinery to all PIC variants helps isolate the effect of the proposed operator. ParPIC also performs strongly on the synthetic chain and core-periphery settings.

Algorithm 1, dataset statistics, SBM parameters, and a code link support reproducibility. The paper openly shows parameter sensitivity, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent for these standard clustering benchmarks.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. For the reversible, irreducible, aperiodic chain P=[[0.9,0.1],[0.8,0.2]] with stationary distribution (8/9,1/9), choosing ν=π makes this a valid P-RW by Proposition 3.2. Nevertheless, the sum of row entropies decreases from 0.8255 for P to 0.7134 for P². The proof incorrectly applies Jensen using P(k,j) as weights over k, although stochasticity only normalizes rows, not columns. This invalidates the claimed monotone entropy curve underlying automatic time selection.

Proposition 3.6 is consequently unsupported and internally inconsistent: Equation 7 defines H as a sum, the proof of Proposition 3.5 inserts a 1/N average, while Equation 10 estimates the sum using N/n. Moreover, the asserted bound H_i(t)≤C(π) follows from the false monotonicity claim; in the counterexample, one row has entropy 0.5004 while H(π)=0.3488.

The claimed domain includes weakly connected graphs with sinks, and the experiments explicitly say PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain sinks, but P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined for zero-outdegree vertices. No dangling-node convention is specified, although stochasticity of P is required by the proofs and algorithm.

The implemented embedding does not match the stated diffusion geometry. Equation 4 uses the weighted norm with factors 1/π(k), whereas Algorithm 1 clusters raw rows of P^t or P^tZ, whose isotropic random projection preserves an unweighted norm. No D_π^{-1/2} correction is used. The Johnson–Lindenstrauss assertion also omits normalization and a precise dimension/error guarantee.

Originality and directional preservation are overstated. D_νP+P^TD_ν is symmetric, so P-RW is ultimately a walk on an undirected weighted graph; directionality is compressed into its weights, and at γ=0 it reduces to normalization of W+W^T. The operator is closely based on Sevi et al. (2025), while power iteration and random projection are established techniques. The principal new entropy component is the part with the invalid theory.

The empirical significance is limited. On k-NN graphs ParPIC merely ties S-PIC in PRB (0.96). Among only two real directed networks, S-PIC slightly exceeds ParPIC on Email-Eu (0.49 versus 0.48), contradicting the claim of consistent superiority, while PolBlogs performance is only 0.39±0.14. The clearest wins are on tailored SBMs with extreme directional probabilities.

The scalability evidence is a single runtime plot without hardware details, asymptotic analysis, error bars, or comparison to modern sparse eigensolvers. Defaults d=n=√N require an N-by-√N embedding and substantial probe computation. Reproducibility is further weakened by unspecified k-NN preprocessing and randomization details and by the DiSBM-CP size discrepancy: Table 5 reports 4000 vertices, whereas three groups of 1300 imply 3900.

Presentation is generally readable, but there is no adequate limitations discussion covering the known-k assumption, graph regularity requirements, loss of orientation information, lack of a clustering-recovery guarantee, or the scaling of √N-dimensional projections. Given the central false theorem and theory–algorithm mismatch, the remaining empirical heuristic is not sufficiently supported for acceptance.

strengths: Presentation: The manuscript is polished and logically organized, with a clear pipeline, readable figures and tables, and substantial appendices. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-yb5wrjmj/call-28f8408f05b7470e97e0a45ed97b387b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Methodological merit: Combining a parametrized reversible walk with power-iteration clustering gives a simple eigen-decomposition-free procedure. Under suitable assumptions, the reversibility and irreducibility properties of the operator are useful, while random projection and sampled-row computations can avoid explicitly storing the full iterated operator.

Evaluation: The paper compares against ten classical directed-graph baselines, reports 100-run means and standard deviations, and covers ten k-NN datasets, three directed SBMs, and two real directed networks. Tables 2–3 show competitive k-NN performance and strong results on the designed directed SBMs.

Analysis and reproducibility: The appendices provide dataset statistics, exact SBM matrices, method descriptions, and extensive sensitivity analyses for the vertex-measure parameter, diffusion time, number of probes, and embedding dimension. A code URL is supplied.

Significance: The problem of scalable clustering on weakly connected directed graphs is useful, and the empirical results suggest that degree-aware reversiblization can help on graphs with strong degree heterogeneity.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive flaw: Proposition 3.5 is false. For the reversible, irreducible, aperiodic chain P=[[0.5,0.5],[0.05,0.95]], which is realizable as P_(pi)=P for an undirected weighted graph, the summed row entropy decreases from H(1)=0.8917 to H(2)=0.8482. The proof incorrectly invokes Jensen's inequality using P(k,j) as weights over k, although stochasticity only ensures that rows—not columns—sum to one. Consequently, the entropy curve need not be monotone and the theoretical rationale for the central automatic time-selection mechanism fails even under favorable assumptions.

The entropy results contain further contradictions. Equation 7 defines H as a sum over rows, whereas the proof of Proposition 3.5 switches to a 1/N average; the stationary limit is therefore off by a factor of N under the stated definition. Proposition 3.6 then uses N/n, appropriate for estimating the sum, while its variance bound relies on the false assertion H_i(t)<=H(pi). No uniform concentration or elbow-stability result connects pointwise entropy estimation to reliable time selection.

Theory–algorithm mismatch: The diffusion distance in Equation 4 weights coordinates by 1/pi, but Algorithm 1 clusters ordinary Euclidean rows of P_(nu)^t or P_(nu)^t Z(0). The stated Johnson–Lindenstrauss argument preserves unweighted row distances, not the defined diffusion distance; an appropriate stationary-distribution weighting would be required. Thus, the diffusion-map theory does not justify the geometry used by the implemented clustering algorithm.

The advertised weakly-connected-graph scope is not established. P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet Section 4 explicitly says PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks; no dangling-node convention is specified. Moreover, weak connectivity and positive nu do not guarantee aperiodicity: a connected bipartite support without self-loops remains periodic, invalidating the asserted convergence used by the entropy method.

Claims of preserving directional dynamics are overstated. D_nu P+P^T D_nu is a symmetric conductance matrix, so the construction is a weighted reversiblization and necessarily discards antisymmetric circulation. On a degree-balanced directed cycle with uniform nu, it reduces to (P+P^T)/2 and cannot distinguish opposite orientations. The paper gives no characterization of which directional information is retained.

Significance of the evidence is limited. On the ten k-NN graphs, ParPIC merely ties S-PIC in aggregate PRB (0.96). Among the two real intrinsically directed graphs, it obtains only 0.39±0.14 on PolBlogs and is slightly worse than S-PIC on Email-Eu (0.48 versus 0.49). The largest gains come from very dense synthetic SBMs constructed around source–sink and degree-heterogeneity patterns favorable to the proposed operator; broader sparse, noisy real-network evidence and significance tests are absent.

The scalability claim is inadequately supported. Figure 3 uses one dense synthetic family and an unspecified 'classical spectral clustering' implementation, without hardware, solver settings, repetitions, error bars, or an accuracy–runtime tradeoff. No formal complexity comparison is given; using sqrt(N) projection dimensions and probes costs roughly O(t|E|sqrt(N)), which is not automatically preferable to a sparse truncated eigensolver computing only k eigenvectors.

Originality is modest: the parametrized reversible operator is credited to prior work, PIC and random projection are established techniques, and Kneedle-based elbow detection is standard. The principal new component appears to be the row-entropy time heuristic, whose core theorem is incorrect.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link. The manuscript does not fully specify sink preprocessing, the exact random-projection distribution and normalization, the time-search horizon and Kneedle settings, k-means configuration, feature preprocessing, or timing hardware and eigensolvers. Algorithm 1 is therefore not a self-contained executable specification.

Limitations and ethics receive insufficient treatment. The paper does acknowledge sensitivity to gamma and degradation as the number of clusters grows, but it lacks a dedicated discussion of reversiblization's information loss, periodic graphs, or limited real-data validation. The impact statement is boilerplate despite experiments involving political and email networks, where privacy and profiling misuse merit brief discussion. No acute ethical concern is apparent, but the treatment is cursory.

Overall assessment: The paper has a discernible method, polished presentation, and substantive experiments, so a Strong Reject would be too severe. However, the false theorem underlying a central claimed contribution, the disconnect between the defined diffusion geometry and the actual embedding, and the insufficiently supported scalability and generality claims require major revision and prevent acceptance.

strengths: Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, and the pipeline, operator construction, Algorithm 1, tables, and extensive appendix make the main proposal easy to follow.

Significance: Combining a parametrized reversible walk with power-iteration clustering is practically appealing. The construction exposes the stationary measure ν+Pᵀν and could provide a useful eigen-free approach for some degree-heterogeneous directed graphs.

Empirical evaluation: The paper compares against ten baselines, reports 100-run results, and includes useful sensitivity analyses for γ, diffusion time, projection dimension, and entropy probes. ParPIC is particularly strong on DiSBM-Chain/CP and improves PolBlogs AMI from the next-best 0.21 to 0.39.
Reproducibility and ethics: Formulas, synthetic-data parameters, and a public code link are provided. The study uses standard clustering benchmarks, and no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. Its Jensen step treats each column of a row-stochastic matrix as normalized weights. For the reversible, aperiodic chain P=[[0.1,0.9],[0.2,0.8]] with stationary distribution (2/11,9/11), the summed row entropy decreases from H(2)=0.9576 to H(3)=0.9473. The proof also alternates between defining H as a sum and an average, omitting a factor N in the limit. Proposition 3.6 subsequently relies on the false bound H_i(t)≤C(π), so its stated variance and concentration bounds are unsupported. This directly affects the central entropy-based time-selection contribution.

Soundness/domain: P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined for sinks, although the paper highlights experiments on graphs containing many sinks and gives no dangling-node convention. Positive ν also does not ensure aperiodicity on a bipartite underlying graph, contrary to the explanatory text. Thus the claimed applicability to arbitrary weakly connected digraphs and the convergence used by the entropy method do not hold as stated.

Soundness/geometry: Equation 4 defines diffusion distance using column weights 1/π, whereas Z=P^tZ(0) preserves ordinary Euclidean distances between rows of P^t. A Johnson–Lindenstrauss projection of P^t therefore does not approximate the claimed diffusion geometry unless π is uniform; a factor such as D_π^{-1/2} is missing.

Scope of directionality: P_(ν) is a walk on symmetric conductances D_νP+PᵀD_ν. Under the default degree-based measure, every balanced/Eulerian digraph reduces to ordinary symmetrization, so the broad claim that the method preserves directional dynamics is overstated. The favorable synthetic tests predominantly emphasize precisely the degree heterogeneity the construction exploits.

Evidence and significance: Only two intrinsically directed real networks are evaluated. ParPIC does not consistently outperform all baselines as claimed: on Email-Eu, S-PIC scores 0.49 versus 0.48, while several methods tie on DiSBM-Baseline. The runtime claim rests on one synthetic family without complexity analysis, hardware, solver details, or error bars; with d and the number of entropy probes both set to √N, the method costs roughly O(t|E|√N), so a general advantage over sparse top-k eigensolvers is not established.

Originality: The reversible operator builds directly on Sevi et al. (2025), PIC is established, and random projection is standard. The main distinct element is the entropy-selection rule, whose theoretical justification is invalid, leaving a useful synthesis but a limited validated methodological advance.

Reproducibility and limitations: The manuscript does not specify the search horizon or KNEEDLE configuration required to select t, sink handling, preprocessing for the K-NN datasets, runtime environment, or whether synthetic graphs were regenerated across runs. The sensitivity appendix honestly shows sharp dependence on (γ,t) for some datasets, but the paper lacks a corresponding limitations discussion. Its impact statement is also cursory regarding privacy or profiling risks for email and social-network applications.

strengths: Significance: Scalable clustering for weakly connected directed graphs is an important problem, and combining reversible diffusion, automatic scale selection, and low-dimensional power iteration could be practically useful.

Soundness—valid component: Equation 3 does define a stochastic random walk on symmetric nonnegative weights, reversible with respect to a measure proportional to ν + Pᵀν; with strictly positive ν and weakly connected support, the irreducibility argument is essentially sound.

Evaluation: The paper compares against ten baselines on ten K-NN datasets, three directed block models, and two real directed networks, reporting 100-run means and standard deviations. The extensive sensitivity studies over γ, diffusion time, projection dimension, and entropy probes are useful. Tables 2–3 show competitive K-NN results and substantial gains on the Chain/Core-Periphery models and PolBlogs.

Presentation: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-5xzxdwhi/call-b509bf5a61224105acb9055ad66359cd/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} has a clear pipeline, readable algorithm, useful dataset statistics, and generally well-organized figures and appendices.

Reproducibility and ethics: The DiSBM matrices, dataset sizes, metrics, and main algorithm are specified, and a code repository is provided. The experiments use standard benchmark-style data and present no apparent material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false for general reversible chains. Its Jensen step incorrectly treats P(k,j) as weights summing to one over k, whereas stochasticity only gives a sum of one over j. For example, the reversible, irreducible, aperiodic chain P=[[0.01,0.99],[0.5,0.5]] has total row entropy approximately 0.749, 1.261, and 1.232 at times 1, 2, and 3, contradicting monotonicity. The proof also switches from the defined sum of row entropies to an average and omits the resulting factor N in the limit.

Proposition 3.6 consequently uses an unjustified bound Hi(t)≤C(π). Although the sampling estimator's unbiasedness is valid, the stated variance and probability bounds are not established as written, and pointwise entropy estimation would not by itself guarantee stable elbow selection. Thus the theoretical foundation for one of the paper's main contributions—the automatic diffusion-time rule—is materially unsound.

There is a mismatch between the proposed diffusion geometry and the implemented algorithm. Equation 4 uses stationary-distribution-weighted distances, while Algorithm 1 clusters ordinary rows of Pᵗ or their random projections, which preserve unweighted row distances. Appendix Equation 19 concerns the spectral embedding ΦΛᵗ and does not show that the actual embedding is isometric to the claimed diffusion distance.

The advertised scope is not fully supported. The natural walk P=Dout⁻¹W is undefined at sinks, yet the paper explicitly says PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks and never specifies a dangling-node convention. Moreover, positivity of ν does not ensure aperiodicity; a weakly connected graph with bipartite support can still produce a periodic P-RW. Consequently, several convergence and ergodicity statements require additional assumptions or a lazy-walk modification.

Originality is modest. The reversible operator is inherited from Sevi et al. (2025), power-iteration clustering and random projections are established techniques, and KNEEDLE supplies the elbow detector. The main novelty is their integration and the row-entropy heuristic, but the principal theorem offered for that heuristic is incorrect.

Claims about preserving directionality need qualification. P-RW is the random walk on the symmetric weight matrix DνP+PᵀDν, so direction affects edge reweighting but directed transition orientation is removed. In balanced regular graphs with constant ν, this reduces to ordinary symmetrization. The paper does not characterize what directional information survives or test direction-reversal/degree-controlled examples.

The empirical claims exceed the evidence. There are only two intrinsically directed real datasets, and Email-Eu has reciprocity 0.72. On K-NN graphs, ParPIC merely ties S-PIC in aggregate PRB (0.96); on Email-Eu it is slightly below S-PIC (0.48 versus 0.49), contrary to the claim of outperforming all baselines. Several differences are small relative to reported standard deviations, without paired significance tests, while the strongest gains occur on synthetic structures aligned with the proposed degree balancing.

Baseline and scalability evidence is incomplete. Missing ablations prevent clean separation of the operator, time selector, and random projection; native baseline tuning is unclear, and the DSC+ fallback using Pᵗ(i,·) is not well-defined independently of i on non-ergodic graphs. Figure 3 uses one synthetic family without hardware, solver, repetition, or timing-scope details. With d and the number of probes both set to √N, iteration can cost O(t|E|√N) and sampled row distributions can densify, so the broad scalability claim is not established.

Presentation and reproducibility are weakened by substantive inconsistencies: Section 2 gives an orthonormal decomposition for a generally nonsymmetric random-walk matrix; the reversibility proof places the diagonal measure on the wrong side of Pᵀ; the entropy normalization changes across sections; and some figure descriptions miscount panels or datasets. The code link helps, but the manuscript omits a version/commit, environment, sink handling, preprocessing and K-NN details, exact γ used in the main tables, and a complete runtime protocol. There is also no candid limitations section covering these assumptions and sensitivities.

Overall, the paper contains a plausible practical idea and substantial experimentation, but a false theorem supporting a central contribution, an unresolved geometry–algorithm mismatch, and insufficiently controlled evidence prevent acceptance in its current form. These are Reject-level rather than merely polish-level revisions.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for the ICML 2026 main research track.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance.

3 = Weak reject
There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly.

4 = Weak accept
The work is technically solid and advances an area in a useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

The evidence does not support the broad superiority claims. On the ten K-NN graphs, ParPIC only ties S-PIC in aggregate PRB and is often numerically worse. Of five intrinsically directed benchmarks, three are synthetic models aligned with the proposed mechanism. On the two real graphs, PolBlogs reaches only 0.39±0.14 AMI, and S-PIC exceeds ParPIC on Email-Eu (0.49 versus 0.48), directly contradicting the claim that ParPIC consistently outperforms every baseline. No significance tests accompany the small differences.

The scalability claim is inadequately evaluated. Figure 3 uses one synthetic family and an unspecified 'classical spectral clustering' implementation, with no hardware, memory, repetitions, error bars, or comparison to optimized sparse eigensolvers. Both the √N-dimensional embedding and √N entropy probes cost roughly O(t|E|√N), which need not beat computation of k eigenvectors when k is small.

Reproducibility remains insufficient despite the code link. Missing details include sink preprocessing, the explicit K and feature standardization for K-NN graphs, real-data filtering, entropy search horizon and KNEEDLE settings, projection distribution and scaling, k-means initialization, seeds, baseline implementations and tuning, and runtime hardware. DiSBM-CP is also reported as 4000 vertices in Table 5 but specified as 3×1300=3900 elsewhere.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies beyond the entropy normalization: the natural random-walk decomposition in Section 2.2 is written as an ordinary orthogonal eigendecomposition although P is generally nonsymmetric; the reversibility proof places the diagonal measure on the wrong side of Pᵀ; and several figure descriptions disagree with the displayed number of datasets. Claims of robustness also sit uneasily with Figure 11's sharp joint sensitivity to γ and t.

Limitations and ethics are treated inadequately. There is no substantive limitations section discussing the restricted real-world evidence, sensitivity, periodicity, or loss of directional information. The boilerplate impact statement dismisses all consequences, despite experiments on political and email networks where privacy, profiling, and cluster-misclassification risks, along with data provenance and licensing, warrant at least brief treatment. These are not necessarily prohibitive ethical concerns, but they are unresolved in the manuscript.

strengths: Soundness: When P is a well-defined transition matrix and the vertex measure is positive, Eq. (3) gives a simple reversible walk with stationary measure proportional to ν+P^Tν; weak connectivity also makes its symmetrized support irreducible.

Significance: Directed-graph clustering is important, and implementing the method through sparse matrix multiplications, sampled entropy estimates, and random projections is potentially useful for moderately large graphs.

Evaluation: The paper reports 100-run results against ten baselines on ten K-NN graphs, multiple directed SBMs, and two real directed networks. ParPIC is particularly strong on the chain/core-periphery SBMs and PolBlogs, while remaining competitive with S-PIC on K-NN graphs.

Presentation: The pipeline and Algorithm 1 are easy to follow, and the appendices provide baseline definitions, dataset statistics, proofs, and extensive sensitivity analyses over γ, diffusion time, probe count, and embedding dimension.

Reproducibility and ethics: A code repository is provided, many experimental parameters are documented, and no material ethical concern is apparent. The sensitivity plots usefully expose substantial dataset-dependent behavior rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. Shannon entropy need not increase under a merely row-stochastic, reversible transition; that property generally requires a doubly stochastic map. The proof incorrectly applies Jensen using P(k,j) as weights even though columns need not sum to one. For example, P=[[0.1,0.9],[0.01,0.99]] and ν=(1,1) satisfy the assumptions and yield P_(ν)≈[[0.180,0.820],[0.315,0.685]], but the stated global entropy decreases from H(2)≈1.1884 to H(3)≈1.1801. The proof also alternates between defining H as a sum and an average; under the stated sum definition its limit is N times the stationary entropy, not the value claimed.

Because Proposition 3.5 fails, the C(π_(ν))-based range and variance bounds in Proposition 3.6 are unsupported; only unbiasedness is established. More broadly, no theorem links an entropy-curve elbow to a clustering-optimal diffusion time, leaving a central claimed contribution as an empirically tested heuristic.

The diffusion theory does not match Algorithm 1. Eq. (4) weights coordinate differences by 1/π_(ν), whereas the algorithm clusters ordinary rows of P_(ν)^t or randomly projects those unweighted rows. To preserve the defined diffusion distance, the projected object should include D_{π_(ν)}^{-1/2}. The stated Johnson–Lindenstrauss approximation also omits the required scaling and precise random-matrix assumptions. Thus, the diffusion-map property in Appendix E does not justify the actual embedding used for clustering.

The advertised graph scope is not properly handled. P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined for sinks, yet the paper emphasizes that PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks; no dangling-node convention is specified. Moreover, positivity of ν and weak connectivity ensure irreducibility but not aperiodicity, contrary to the prose after Proposition 3.2. The appendix proves only the sufficient self-loop case, so power iterations can oscillate on bipartite support graphs.

Originality is modest and insufficiently delineated. Eq. (3) is a random walk on the symmetric conductance matrix D_νP+P^TD_ν and is closely tied to the cited generalized-Laplacian construction of Sevi et al. The other ingredients are a standard random projection and a heuristic knee detector. Since orientation is compressed into symmetric edge weights, claims that the resulting walk “preserves directional dynamics” need qualification.

The empirical evidence is not broad enough for the general claims. Only two intrinsically directed real networks are used, the strongest gains occur on favorable synthetic degree/flow constructions, and ParPIC is not best on Email-Eu despite claims of consistent superiority. Comparisons also mix methods designed for different clustering objectives, while the very large gap between GSC and ParPIC using related operators is not investigated.

The scalability claim is under-supported. Figure 3 omits hardware, solver details, repeated-run uncertainty, and comparisons with scalable sparse eigensolvers. With both projection dimension and entropy probes set to √N, the principal work is approximately O(tE√N), so an eigen-free implementation is not automatically cheaper than computing k eigenvectors when k is small.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: the manuscript omits the K-NN value and feature preprocessing, sink handling, main-table γ settings, time-search horizon and full KNEEDLE configuration, projection distribution/normalization, k-means restart settings, seeds, and runtime hardware. The DiSBM-CP specification also gives 3×1300=3900 vertices while Table 5 reports 4000.

There is no substantive limitations discussion covering the false entropy assumption, loss of orientation through reversibilization, parameter sensitivity, or asymptotic cost. The impact statement is boilerplate; although not a material ethical blocker, community inference on political and communication networks warrants brief discussion of privacy and potential misuse.

strengths: Soundness: The construction in Eq. 3 has a useful interpretation as a reversible random walk with stationary measure proportional to ν + Pᵀν; the stochasticity, reversibility, and weak-connectivity-to-irreducibility arguments are largely straightforward and valuable.

Originality: Combining the parametrized operator with PIC, sampled entropy-based time selection, and matrix-valued random projections forms a coherent pipeline, even though the individual ingredients are mostly established.

Significance: Scalable clustering of weakly connected directed graphs is important, and avoiding eigendecomposition could be practically useful. ParPIC ties S-PIC on the ten K-NN datasets and shows substantial gains on the tailored degree-heterogeneous DiSBMs.
Evaluation and reproducibility: The paper reports AMI with variability over 100 runs, multiple sensitivity studies, explicit DiSBM matrices, several baseline families, and a public code URL.

Presentation and ethics: The manuscript is professionally organized with a clear algorithm and readable figures. The task poses no evident material ethical risk, and the paper includes an impact statement. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-_oo1652r/call-d745c3b1904a4effb40f43fac69d403a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. Its Jensen step treats P(k,j) as normalized weights over k, but a row-stochastic matrix need not have unit column sums. A counterexample within the paper's own reversible, aperiodic setting is P=[[0.9,0.1],[0.8,0.2]], with stationary distribution (8/9,1/9): the sum of row entropies decreases from approximately 0.825 at t=1 to 0.713 at t=2. Thus the proposed entropy curve is not generally monotone.

Soundness: Eq. 7 defines H as a sum of N row entropies, so its limit is N times the stationary entropy, not the stationary entropy asserted in Proposition 3.5. The appendix silently changes H to an average before reverting to the sum in Proposition 3.6. Moreover, the variance bound in Proposition 3.6 relies on the false claim that each transient row entropy is bounded by the stationary entropy; only unbiasedness is established. A pointwise Chebyshev bound would not by itself guarantee stable data-dependent elbow selection.

Soundness: The theory and implemented embedding do not match. Eq. 4 uses the weighted distance ‖(Pᵗ(i,·)−Pᵗ(j,·))Dπ⁻¹ᐟ²‖, whereas Algorithm 1 clusters unweighted rows of Pᵗ or PᵗZ₀. The stated Johnson–Lindenstrauss argument therefore preserves a different distance from the claimed diffusion geometry unless the stationary distribution is uniform.

Soundness and scope: Strict positivity of ν does not ensure aperiodicity; a weakly connected bipartite support without self-loops remains period two. The proof only treats the self-loop case, while the abstract and surrounding text claim broad coverage of weakly connected digraphs. More seriously, P=Dout⁻¹W is undefined at sinks, yet the paper explicitly says PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks and gives no dangling-node convention. Leaving zero rows would invalidate the stochasticity and convergence proofs.

Originality: The operator is closely based on the authors' prior generalized-Laplacian construction, PIC and random projection are established, and the degree-mixture measure is simple. Eq. 3 is exactly a walk on symmetric conductances νᵢPᵢⱼ+νⱼPⱼᵢ; for balanced in/out degrees it reduces to a conventional symmetrized walk. Consequently, the repeated claim that it preserves directional dynamics needs a formal qualification, especially because circulation information is necessarily lost.

Significance and evidence: Most real-data evidence is weak: the ten K-NN directions are artificial and ParPIC merely ties S-PIC; only two small natural networks are tested, and on Email-Eu S-PIC slightly exceeds ParPIC (0.49 versus 0.48), contradicting the claim of outperforming all baselines. The largest gains occur on synthetic models designed around the degree heterogeneity the proposed weighting corrects. Large real graphs and directionality-controlled tests are absent.

Reproducibility and presentation: Important details are missing or inconsistent, including K-NN preprocessing and K, sink handling, the main-table γ setting, entropy search horizon and KNEEDLE configuration, spectral/complex embedding details, random-seed protocol, and runtime hardware and included operations. DiSBM-CP is listed as 4000 vertices although 3×1300=3900. The scalability claim rests on one synthetic runtime plot without uncertainty or comparable directed baselines.

Limitations and ethics: The sensitivity analysis is useful, but there is no substantive limitations discussion covering loss of orientation under reversibilization, required knowledge of k, periodic graphs, sink treatment, or O(N√N) embedding storage. The generic impact statement is acceptable for this low-risk method, though dataset provenance and licensing are not documented. Overall, the false theorem supporting the central time-selection contribution and the geometry/implementation mismatch are material deficiencies that prevent acceptance.
