strengths: Soundness: Equation 3 gives a transparent construction whose stochasticity, reversibility with respect to ν + P^Tν, and irreducibility on a weakly connected support are largely well motivated when the natural random walk is well-defined.

Significance: An eigen-free clustering pipeline for directed graphs is practically relevant. Combining iterative diffusion, randomized low-dimensional embeddings, sampled time selection, and k-means is computationally appealing.

Evaluation: The paper reports 100-run results against ten baselines, targeted DiSBM studies, and sensitivity analyses for γ, diffusion time, probe count, and embedding dimension. ParPIC ties S-PIC at PRB 0.96 on the ten k-NN datasets and performs strongly on DiSBM-Chain, DiSBM-CP, and PolBlogs.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main narrative, pipeline diagram, pseudocode, dataset statistics, and appendices are generally well organized. Providing a public code link is valuable, and the sensitivity analysis candidly shows that γ and t can substantially affect performance.

Originality and ethics: Integrating the prior parametrized reversibilization with a matrix-valued PIC implementation and sampled entropy heuristic is a coherent contribution. The application is low-risk, and no unresolved material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false for a general reversible stochastic matrix. Its Jensen step treats P(k,j) as weights summing to one over k, whereas row-stochasticity only gives a sum over j. For example, the ergodic reversible matrix [[0.1,0.9],[0.01,0.99]] has summed row entropy about 0.381 at t=1 and 0.154 at t=2. The paper also inconsistently defines H as a sum versus an average and omits the corresponding factor N in its limit. Consequently, the C(π)-based variance and concentration bounds in Proposition 3.6 are unsupported. This directly affects the claimed theoretical basis of a central contribution, automatic diffusion-time selection; moreover, no result connects an entropy elbow to a cluster-optimal time.

Soundness and scope: The method is not defined for all graphs it claims to handle. P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet the paper explicitly emphasizes that PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks and gives no dangling-node convention. A positive ν cannot repair an undefined P. The text also incorrectly suggests that positivity of ν alone ensures aperiodicity; additional support conditions are required.

Theory–algorithm mismatch: Equation 4 defines diffusion distance using coordinate weights 1/π, but Algorithm 1 clusters ordinary Euclidean rows of P^t or their unweighted random projections. Preserving the stated diffusion distance would require projecting appropriately π-weighted rows. The claimed Johnson–Lindenstrauss approximation also omits normalization of the Gaussian or uniform projection, so the displayed near-equality is not correct as written. Thus, the diffusion-geometry development does not justify the implemented embedding, especially in the degree-heterogeneous regime where π is nonuniform.

Significance and evidence: Broad claims of consistent superiority on directed networks are not supported by sufficiently broad real-world evidence. Only two small intrinsically directed real graphs are tested; ParPIC improves on PolBlogs but trails S-PIC on Email-Eu, 0.48 versus 0.49. The other large gains come from three synthetic structures closely aligned with the proposed operator's motivating failure mode, while ParPIC offers essentially no advantage over symmetrization on the ten k-NN graphs. Standard directed community-detection alternatives are absent.

Scalability: Figure 3 is a single synthetic comparison against an unspecified “classical spectral clustering” implementation, without hardware, uncertainty, memory measurements, or comparisons to the other eigen-free baselines and modern sparse eigensolvers. With both the sketch dimension and entropy-probe count set to √N, the stated procedure can require roughly O(tE√N) work and O(N√N) dense storage. No complexity analysis substantiates the general scalability claims, including the claimed advantage over teleportation-based methods.

Reproducibility and baseline validity: Important details are missing, including the k-NN value and feature preprocessing, dataset versions/provenance, sink handling, the time-search horizon and KNEEDLE settings, k-means configuration, random-seed protocol, and what randomness the reported 100 runs average over. Baseline definitions also contain serious ambiguities: as written, Simple-Herm's reverse-edge case multiplies W_ij under the condition W_ij=0, and its D^{1/2}SD^{-1/2} normalization is not generally Hermitian. Section 4.1 names PR-SC, but it does not appear in the tables or implementation description.

Originality: The reversible operator is inherited from the authors' prior generalized-Laplacian work, PIC and random projection are established techniques, and using multiple projection columns is a straightforward extension. The main distinctive element is therefore the entropy heuristic, whose principal theorem is incorrect and which has neither a recovery guarantee nor a formal relationship to k-cluster structure.

Presentation and limitations: The prose is mostly clear, but several claims are mathematically imprecise, many appendix plots have very small labels, and notation alternates between sums and averages or between N and n. There is no substantive limitations discussion covering sinks, bipartite/periodic graphs, loss of directional flow under reversibilization, parameter-sensitive failure cases, or the limited real-world evaluation. The generic impact statement is acceptable for this low-risk topic but does not compensate for the missing methodological limitations.

strengths: Presentation is generally clear and polished: Figure 1, Algorithm 1, the notation table, and the appendices make the complete pipeline easy to follow. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2lq0r5n6/call-e990f6e44d8443538af31a0bbc8e04c4/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

For a row-stochastic P and strictly positive vertex measure, the proposed operator has a simple probabilistic interpretation; the symmetry of DνP+PᵀDν supports reversibility, while weak connectivity yields irreducibility of its symmetrized support.

The evaluation covers ten K-NN datasets, three directed-SBM settings, two real directed networks, ten baselines, repeated trials, and extensive sensitivity analyses for γ, diffusion time, projection dimension, and entropy probes. Results on chain and core-periphery SBMs provide useful evidence under directional degree heterogeneity.

Avoiding explicit eigendecomposition could be practically useful, and applying the proposed time-selection and projection machinery to all PIC baselines helps isolate the effect of the P-RW operator. Code is linked, and no acute research-ethics concern arises from the standard benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: The decisive soundness problem is that Proposition 3.5 is false. Reversibility does not make a transition matrix column-stochastic, yet the Jensen step treats {P(k,j)} over k as normalized weights. For the reversible, irreducible, aperiodic matrix P=[[0.1,0.9],[0.4,0.6]], the summed row entropy decreases from 1.2519 at t=2 to 1.2251 at t=3. Consequently, the claimed monotonicity and the theoretical rationale for elbow-based time selection are unsupported.

Related entropy results are internally inconsistent. H is defined as a sum of N row entropies, but the proof switches to an average and gives a limit missing a factor N. Proposition 3.6's concentration bound also uses the invalid assertion that every row entropy is bounded by the stationary-distribution entropy; only its unbiasedness calculation remains justified as written.

The claimed applicability to graphs containing sinks is not defined. The method starts from P=Dout⁻¹W, which is undefined when an out-degree is zero, even though PolBlogs and Email-Eu are explicitly said to contain sinks. Treating dangling rows as zero would make P non-stochastic and invalidate Proposition 3.2. No self-loop or dangling-node convention is provided.

The practical embedding is not shown to implement the stated diffusion geometry. Equation 4 uses π⁻¹-weighted row distances, whereas PᵗZ with an ordinary random projection preserves unweighted Euclidean distances between rows of Pᵗ. No Dπ⁻¹/² correction is used, and the projection distribution and normalization needed for a Johnson–Lindenstrauss guarantee are unspecified.

The evidence for broad real-world benefit is limited. The only intrinsically directed real graphs each have roughly one thousand vertices; ParPIC is slightly worse than S-PIC on Email-Eu (0.48 versus 0.49 AMI), and it ties S-PIC in aggregate on the K-NN graphs (PRB 0.96). The largest improvements occur on tailored synthetic chain and core-periphery models, so claims of consistent superiority are overstated.

The scalability claim rests on one runtime plot against an unspecified classical spectral-clustering implementation, without hardware details, variability, memory measurements, complexity analysis, or comparison to the other scalable PIC methods. With both probe count and embedding dimension set to √N, the default implementation requires dense O(N√N) storage and O(tm√N) work, which is not compelling for genuinely large sparse graphs.

Originality is modest: the reversible operator builds directly on Sevi et al. (2025), while PIC and random projections are established techniques. The main new entropy selector has an invalid theorem, leaving primarily an empirical integration of known components.

Reproducibility and limitations treatment are inadequate despite the code link: the manuscript omits critical sink handling, the explicit K-NN choice and preprocessing, the time-search horizon and KNEEDLE configuration, projection scaling, clustering settings, baseline-tuning protocol, and runtime environment. It also lacks a candid limitations discussion; the generic impact statement does not address privacy or profiling risks from community detection. These issues require substantial correction before others can reliably build on the work.

Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

1 = Strong Reject
The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance.

3 = Weak reject
There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly.

4 = Weak accept
The work is technically solid and advances an area in a useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

strengths: Presentation: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-vfd7hhng/call-a0555a720fb1427d8169d37a2a2b5998/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} is clearly organized, with an intuitive pipeline diagram, pseudocode, notation table, and readable appendices.

Soundness—core construction: The algebra showing that P_(ν) is stochastic, reversible with respect to ν+Pᵀν, and irreducible on a weakly connected support is useful and largely convincing under the required positivity and well-definedness assumptions.

Evaluation: The paper compares against ten baselines on ten k-NN graphs, three directed SBMs, and two real directed networks; reports AMI variability over repeated runs; and includes extensive sensitivity analyses for γ, diffusion time, probe count, and embedding dimension.

Significance: An eigen-decomposition-free clustering pipeline for directed, non-strongly-connected graphs is practically relevant. ParPIC performs particularly well on the tailored chain and core-periphery models and improves substantially on PolBlogs.

Reproducibility and ethics: Synthetic-model parameters and most algorithmic defaults are documented, and a public code repository is provided. The work has limited direct ethical risk and no unresolved material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive issue: Proposition 3.5 is false for general reversible row-stochastic matrices. The Jensen step treats P(k,j) as weights over k although their sum need not equal one; entropy is guaranteed to increase under doubly stochastic, not merely reversible, transitions. For example, the reversible ergodic matrix [[0.9,0.1],[0.8,0.2]] has summed row entropy about 0.825 at t=1 and 0.713 at t=2. Thus the claimed monotonic entropy curve, which motivates automatic diffusion-time selection, lacks theoretical support.

Proposition 3.6 consequently uses an invalid bound H_i(t)≤C(π): transient entropy can exceed stationary entropy. There is also a normalization contradiction—Eq. 7 defines H as a sum, its proof switches to an average, and the stated limit omits the resulting factor N—while the sampling estimator again targets the sum.

The claimed scope is not established. P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet the paper emphasizes datasets containing many sinks without specifying a dangling-node rule. Strict positivity of ν also does not guarantee aperiodicity; weakly connected bipartite graphs remain periodic, contradicting surrounding claims of convergence for weakly connected digraphs generally.

The implemented embedding does not match the developed diffusion geometry: diffusion distance weights columns by 1/π_(ν), whereas clustering raw rows of P_(ν)^t or P_(ν)^tZ⁽⁰⁾ preserves, at best, unweighted row distances. The Johnson–Lindenstrauss claim also omits normalization, distributional conditions, distortion, and probability guarantees.

The empirical advantage is narrower than the prose suggests. On the ten k-NN datasets ParPIC merely ties S-PIC in aggregate; among the two real directed networks it improves PolBlogs but slightly loses to S-PIC on Email-Eu. The strongest gains occur on synthetic models constructed around the proposed method’s core-periphery/flow motivation, and no significance tests support claims of consistent superiority.

The scalability claim is insufficiently substantiated: there is no asymptotic analysis, hardware or implementation description, uncertainty reporting, or accuracy–runtime comparison. With d and the number of entropy probes both set to √N, sparse iterations can cost roughly O(t|E|√N) time and O(N√N) memory, so superiority to modern partial eigensolvers is not automatic. Figure 3 compares against only an unspecified classical spectral implementation on one synthetic family.

Originality is modest: the reversible vertex-measure operator is inherited from Sevi et al., power-iteration clustering from Lin and Cohen, and random projection is standard. Their integration is useful, but the main distinct ingredient—the entropy time selector—is precisely the component with the invalid theorem.

Reproducibility and limitations treatment remain incomplete: the manuscript omits explicit sink handling, feature preprocessing, the stated value of K for k-NN construction, random-projection scaling, KNEEDLE range/settings, k-means settings, seeds, and runtime environment. It has no substantive limitations discussion, and its impact statement is boilerplate. Moreover, the supplied version exposes authors, affiliations, acknowledgments, arXiv metadata, and a named repository, so it is not suitable as a double-blind ICML submission. Because a central theoretical claim is false and several headline scope/scalability claims are unsupported, these issues require more than a minor revision.

Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance.

3 = Weak reject
There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly.

4 = Weak accept
The work is technically solid and advances an area in a useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

strengths: Presentation: The manuscript is clearly organized and well motivated, with an accessible pipeline diagram, explicit algorithm, readable notation, and substantial appendices covering proofs and experimental details. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-okxsjazq/call-9a14c846b1d246979350b642537553cd/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Significance: Scalable clustering of weakly connected directed graphs is an important problem. Replacing eigendecomposition with sparse operator applications and sampled-row calculations could be practically useful.

Empirical scope: The evaluation includes ten k-NN graphs, two intrinsically directed real networks, three synthetic models, ten baselines, repeated trials, and sensitivity analyses for gamma, diffusion time, projection dimension, and probe count.

Originality: Combining a parametrized reversible operator with power-iteration clustering and an automatic row-entropy scale selector is a coherent integration, even though most individual ingredients are established.

Reproducibility and ethics: The paper supplies synthetic-model matrices, dataset statistics, baseline formulas, and a code URL. No material ethical issue is apparent for this benchmark study, although the impact discussion is cursory.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. Its Jensen step treats P(k,j) as weights over k, but those values need not sum to one because a stochastic matrix need not be doubly stochastic. For example, the reversible, positive, aperiodic chain P=[[0.1,0.9],[0.2,0.8]]—also realizable as P_(pi) for an undirected weighted graph—has summed row entropies 0.9576 at t=2 and 0.9473 at t=3. Thus entropy is not necessarily non-decreasing, undermining the principal theoretical justification for the proposed time selector.

Soundness: Equation 7 defines H as a sum over vertices, whereas the proof of Proposition 3.5 silently changes it to an average; the limit of the sum would be N times the stationary entropy. Proposition 3.6 further assumes each transient row entropy is bounded by the stationary entropy, which the same counterexample disproves. Consequently, its stated variance and concentration bounds do not follow, although unbiasedness itself does.

Method definition: The natural walk P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet the paper explicitly emphasizes that PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks and never gives a dangling-node convention. Treating sink rows as zero would invalidate stochasticity and the subsequent proofs. Likewise, positivity of nu and weak connectivity do not ensure aperiodicity on a bipartite support; the proof only establishes a sufficient self-loop condition, contrary to the surrounding claims.

Theory–algorithm mismatch: The diffusion distance in Equation 4 weights columns by 1/pi(k), but Algorithm 1 clusters unweighted rows of P_(nu)^t. The random projection in Equation 8 preserves ordinary row distances, not this weighted diffusion distance; a factor such as D_pi^{-1/2} would be needed. The diffusion-map proposition therefore does not justify the embedding actually used.

Originality and interpretation: The P-RW operator is inherited from Sevi et al. (2025), PIC and random projection are established, and the remaining major novelty—the entropy selector—has invalid theory. Moreover, P-RW is exactly a random walk on symmetric conductances c_ij=nu_i P_ij+nu_j P_ji; the manuscript does not formalize what directional information this reversibilization preserves, making repeated claims of preserving directionality too strong.

Evidence and significance: The largest gains occur on dense, extreme DiSBMs designed around the degree asymmetries the operator corrects. There are only two intrinsically directed real datasets; ParPIC loses slightly to S-PIC on Email-Eu (0.48 versus 0.49) and merely ties S-PIC in aggregate on the k-NN suite. The broad superiority claim is therefore not established, and no paired significance tests are reported.

Evaluation fairness and scalability: Power-iteration methods use d≈√N random features while spectral methods appear to use only k eigenvectors, confounding operator and representation capacity. The very poor result of the spectral GSC baseline built from the same P-RW family is not investigated. The sole runtime plot lacks hardware, solver, repetition, and uncertainty details, and there is no complexity analysis acknowledging the O(t|E|√N) work and O(N√N) embedding storage or comparison with modern sparse eigensolvers.

Reproducibility and presentation: Important choices are missing or ambiguous, including sink handling, k-NN preprocessing and K, the diffusion-time search horizon and KNEEDLE settings, random-projection normalization, k-means restarts, seeds, eigensolvers, baseline tuning, and runtime hardware. There are also internal inconsistencies such as 4,000 versus 3×1,300 vertices for DiSBM-CP and the sum/average definition of H.

Limitations and ethics: There is no substantive limitations section acknowledging the invalid or restrictive assumptions, sensitivity and failure cases, dependence on known k, limited real-network evidence, or subquadratic-but-superlinear storage. The generic impact statement also overlooks privacy and profiling considerations when clustering social or email networks, although no unresolved major ethical concern is evident.

strengths: Presentation: The paper is well organized, with a clear algorithm, notation table, dataset statistics, baseline definitions, and generally polished figures. The appendix usefully exposes parameter sensitivities. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ggnao6uq/call-b05b4f09c31647d586fb300711d8bac3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Method and significance: Combining a degree-parametrized reversible operator with power-iteration clustering is computationally appealing. The vertex measure offers an interpretable way to control in-degree versus out-degree information.

Empirical evidence: The evaluation includes ten k-NN datasets, three directed SBMs, and two real directed networks, with 100-run summaries and sensitivity studies. ParPIC is especially strong on DiSBM-Chain, DiSBM-CP, and PolBlogs, and Figure 3 suggests useful runtime gains.

Limitations and reproducibility: The authors appropriately acknowledge that directionality gives little advantage on highly reciprocal k-NN graphs and document sensitivity to gamma, diffusion time, and embedding dimension. Equations, pseudocode, defaults, and a public code link aid replication; no material ethical concern is apparent for these standard graph-clustering benchmarks.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false for general reversible, aperiodic chains. For example, P=[[0.1,0.9],[0.2,0.8]] is reversible and aperiodic, and is realizable as P_(pi), yet its summed row entropy decreases from 0.9576 at t=2 to 0.9473 at t=3. The proof misuses Jensen's inequality because the purported weights P(k,j) need not sum to one over k. It also changes H from a sum in Eq. 7 to an average in the proof, producing an inconsistent limiting constant.

Proposition 3.6 consequently has an invalid variance and concentration bound: the asserted bound H_i(t)<=C(pi) relies on Proposition 3.5 and fails when a transient row has greater entropy than the nonuniform stationary distribution. Only the unbiasedness calculation remains valid. Moreover, no theory connects the KNEEDLE entropy elbow to a clustering-optimal diffusion time.

The implemented embedding does not match the defined diffusion geometry. Equation 4 weights coordinates by 1/pi_(nu), whereas the random projection in Section 3.5 preserves ordinary Euclidean distances between raw rows of P_(nu)^t. These coincide only in special cases such as uniform stationary measure, so the claim that Algorithm 1 faithfully approximates the proposed diffusion map is unsupported.

The directionality claim is overstated. P_(nu) is exactly a random walk on the symmetric weighted adjacency D_nu P + P^T D_nu; it may retain orientation-dependent weights, but its resulting dynamics are reversible and contain no directed stationary flow. This also limits originality: the operator comes from closely related prior work, while power iteration, random projections, and knee detection are established ingredients.

The stated scope is incomplete. Weak connectivity and positive nu do not ensure aperiodicity; a weakly connected bipartite graph remains period two, despite the text claiming positivity ensures both irreducibility and aperiodicity. More seriously, P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, although the paper emphasizes datasets containing many sinks and never specifies a dangling-node convention.

The experimental evidence does not support the broad superiority claims. The strongest gains occur on hand-designed SBMs aligned with the method; there are only two intrinsically directed real datasets, and ParPIC loses slightly to S-PIC on Email-Eu (0.48 versus 0.49). On the ten k-NN datasets it ties S-PIC at PRB 0.96. Statistical tests and broader directed-community regimes are absent.

The scalability and reproducibility evidence is incomplete. Figure 3 compares only against an unspecified 'classical spectral clustering' implementation on one synthetic family, without hardware, memory, asymptotic analysis, or scalable sparse eigensolver baselines; the default N-by-sqrt(N) embedding itself uses O(N^{3/2}) memory. Exact k-NN preprocessing, the projection distribution, main-table gamma choice, KNEEDLE search range/settings, k-means restarts, sink handling, and runtime environment are also unspecified. The generic impact statement and lack of a dedicated limitations discussion miss these material restrictions.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for the ICML 2026 main research track.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance.

3 = Weak reject
There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly.

4 = Weak accept
The work is technically solid and advances an area in a useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

strengths: Soundness: Given a valid stochastic P and strictly positive measure, Eq. 3 provides an intuitive symmetric-conductance random walk; the stochasticity, reversibility, and weak-connectivity-to-irreducibility arguments are largely straightforward.

Significance: Efficient clustering of weakly connected directed graphs is useful, and avoiding a full eigendecomposition through repeated operator applications and random projections is practically motivated.

Evaluation: The paper compares 10 baselines on 10 k-NN datasets, three directed SBMs, and two real directed networks, reporting 100-run means and standard deviations. ParPIC shows notable gains on DiSBM-Chain, DiSBM-CP, and PolBlogs in Table 3, while the extensive parameter studies expose sensitivity to gamma, diffusion time, projection dimension, and entropy sampling.

Presentation: The pipeline, Algorithm 1, tables, and appendices are organized clearly and rendered professionally. The manuscript includes proofs, dataset statistics, implementation descriptions, and a public code link. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-3ieb6g3x/call-0841dd4d42724709b1cf8f15e620c71e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
Ethics: No material ethical concern is apparent for this methodological work using synthetic and standard benchmark graphs, although the impact discussion is minimal.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. Appendix E applies Jensen using P(k,j) as weights without the required column-sum condition; row stochasticity only gives sum_j P(k,j)=1. For the admissible irreducible, aperiodic, reversible chain P=[[0.95,0.05],[0.75,0.25]], the stated row-entropy sum decreases from H(1)=0.761 to H(2)=0.552. Thus the theoretical basis of the automatic diffusion-time contribution fails.

Proposition 3.6 consequently uses an invalid bound H_i(t)<=C(pi). There is also an unresolved normalization contradiction: Eq. 7 defines H as a sum, its proof silently changes it to an average and gives the limit as one stationary entropy, while Eq. 10 again estimates the sum. The pointwise Chebyshev bound would not in any case guarantee stable recovery of a KNEEDLE elbow.

The practical embedding is not the diffusion embedding justified by Eq. 4. That distance weights columns by 1/pi_(nu), whereas Algorithm 1 clusters raw rows of P_(nu)^t and Eq. 8's projection preserves their unweighted Euclidean distances. A D_pi^{-1/2} weighting or corresponding projection is needed; this mismatch is especially consequential on the heterogeneous-degree graphs emphasized by the paper.

The claimed graph scope is not technically handled. P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet Sec. 4.1 explicitly says the real graphs contain many sinks and never specifies dangling-node treatment. Weak connectivity and positive nu also do not ensure aperiodicity, contrary to the paragraph after Proposition 3.2; Appendix E proves only the sufficient self-loop case. Without aperiodicity, convergence and the entropy curve can fail.

Originality is modest: the work combines the earlier vertex-measure reversible construction, PIC, standard random projections, and KNEEDLE. Moreover, P_(nu) is itself a walk on the symmetric conductance D_nu P+P^T D_nu, so it retains direction only indirectly; at gamma=0 it reduces exactly to the normalized W+W^T walk. Claims that it preserves directional dynamics should therefore be qualified.

The scalability claim lacks an asymptotic analysis and convincing controls. With the default d=n=sqrt(N), embedding and entropy estimation can require O(t|E|sqrt(N)) work and O(Nsqrt(N)) dense storage, potentially exceeding a sparse k-eigenvector solver when k is small. Figure 3 reports one dense synthetic family without hardware, repetitions, error bars, or clarity about whether time-selection cost is included.

Empirical reach is limited by only two small real directed networks. ParPIC ties S-PIC in aggregate on k-NN graphs and is slightly worse on Email-Eu (0.48 versus 0.49), contradicting statements that it consistently outperforms every competitor. PolBlogs performance remains modest (0.39 AMI), no significance tests are supplied, and the strongest results come from tailored SBMs.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: feature preprocessing and K for k-NN graphs, real-data provenance, dangling-node handling, main-table gamma settings, random-projection scaling, k-means configuration, seeds, KNEEDLE horizon/settings, and runtime hardware are omitted. DSC+'s fallback uses P^t(i,.) for an unspecified i and 'sufficiently large' t, and the displayed Simple-Herm definition uses W_ij in a branch requiring W_ij=0.

Limitations are not treated adequately. There is no dedicated discussion of reversible information loss, known-k dependence, periodic graphs, unfavorable complexity regimes, parameter sensitivity, or the narrow real-data evaluation; the impact statement is boilerplate rather than a substantive consideration of possible misuse or privacy implications of network community inference.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem with a clear, coherent eigen-free clustering pipeline and generally polished presentation. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8y9pqh5j/call-53f256704d56495da882c7f259a257e5/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Under a valid row-stochastic P and strictly positive measure, Eq. (3) does produce a reversible Markov operator with stationary measure proportional to ν+P^Tν; the associated weighted spectral identity is useful.
The evaluation covers ten K-NN datasets, three directed SBMs, two real directed networks, ten baselines, 100-run variability, parameter sensitivities, and scaling to 30,000 vertices.
Giving every PIC variant the same time-selection and projection machinery is a thoughtful control that helps isolate differences between transition operators.
ParPIC performs particularly well on the synthetic chain and core-periphery models, and the manuscript provides code plus many dataset and model parameters.
weaknesses: The central entropy theorem is incorrect. In Proposition 3.5, Jensen's inequality treats P(k,j) as normalized weights over k, but row-stochasticity only normalizes over j. Entropy need not increase for a reversible, non-doubly-stochastic chain. The claimed stationary limit also requires aperiodicity, which the proposition omits; a reversible two-state cycle is an immediate counterexample.

Proposition 3.6 consequently uses an unjustified bound H_i(t)≤C(π). There is also a normalization contradiction: Section 3.4 and the estimator define H as a sum over vertices, whereas the proof switches to an average and reports H(π), rather than N H(π), as its limit. These errors undermine the automatic time-selection contribution and its sampling guarantee.

The displayed algorithm is undefined on some evaluated graphs. P=D_out^{-1}W requires every vertex to have positive out-degree, yet the paper explicitly says PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks. No dangling-node correction or preprocessing is specified; retaining zero rows would also invalidate the proof that P_(ν) is stochastic.

The implemented embedding is not shown to realize the proposed diffusion geometry. The diffusion distance weights coordinates by 1/π, whereas Algorithm 1 and its random projection preserve ordinary Euclidean distances between rows of P_(ν)^t. A π^{-1/2} column scaling or another justification is needed, along with precise projection normalization and guarantees.

Originality is limited by the fact that the reversible operator builds directly on Sevi et al. and power-iteration clustering and random projection are established ideas. Moreover, D_νP+P^TD_ν is symmetric, so the method ultimately performs a reversible walk on bidirectionalized support; claims of preserving asymmetric flow dynamics need a more precise qualification.

Several empirical claims are overstated. ParPIC ties S-PIC in aggregate on K-NN graphs and is lower on many individual datasets; on Email-Eu, S-PIC scores 0.49 versus ParPIC's 0.48. Evidence on intrinsically directed real data comprises only two networks, with PolBlogs showing 0.39±0.14, while the strongest gains occur on tailored synthetic structures.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: feature normalization, explicit K, sink handling, graph preprocessing, random seeds, k-means settings, the sources of the 100-run randomness, and full KNEEDLE configuration are not reported. The runtime study also omits hardware, variability, precise included stages, and comparisons with scalable directed alternatives.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations discussion covering known k, positivity/aperiodicity assumptions, dangling vertices, and the cost of entropy estimation. The generic impact statement also overlooks privacy or sensitive-community inference concerns associated with clustering email and political networks.

strengths: The paper is clearly motivated and presents an accessible pipeline combining a parametrized reversible operator, power iteration, time selection, random projection, and k-means.

Assuming a valid stochastic P and strictly positive measure, the construction P_(ν) is simple, interpretable as a normalized symmetric conductance matrix, and the reversibility and weak-connectivity-to-irreducibility arguments are useful.

The evaluation covers ten k-NN graphs, three directed SBMs, and two real networks, reports variability over repeated runs, and includes extensive sensitivity analyses for γ, diffusion time, sampling, and embedding dimension.

ParPIC is competitive on the k-NN benchmarks and substantially improves results on the tailored chain and core-periphery SBMs. Applying the proposed time selector and projection to all PIC variants is a sensible attempt to isolate the operator's effect.
Code is linked, the manuscript candidly notes regimes where symmetrization is equally effective and where γ matters, and the work raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 3.5 is false. Shannon entropy need not increase when a distribution is multiplied by a reversible row-stochastic matrix. For example, the reversible, irreducible, aperiodic matrix [[0.1,0.9],[0.01,0.99]] gives summed row entropy 0.381 at t=1 and 0.154 at t=2. The Jensen step incorrectly treats each column P(k,j) as normalized weights. This directly undermines the theoretical basis of the central entropy time selector.

The false monotonicity also invalidates the bound H_i(t)≤C(π) used in Proposition 3.6. Moreover, Eq. 7 defines H as a sum, whereas the proof uses an average; the stated limit and the N/n sampling estimator cannot both be correct under these definitions.

The claimed applicability to graphs with sinks is not well-defined: P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined for zero-out-degree vertices, yet the paper explicitly says PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks and specifies no dangling-node convention. Similarly, positive ν does not ensure aperiodicity; a weakly connected graph with bipartite support yields an oscillating P_(ν), contradicting the convergence-based claims unless the chain is lazified.

The implemented random projection does not preserve the paper's stated diffusion distance. Eq. 4 uses the weighted norm of P_(ν)^t rows with weights 1/π_(ν), while Z=P_(ν)^tZ(0) preserves ordinary unweighted row distances. A D_π^{-1/2} column weighting or a separate justification is required.

Originality is limited: the parametrized operator is inherited from Sevi et al. (2025), power-iteration clustering and random projection are established tools, and the principal new time-selection component rests on the incorrect theorem.

The empirical evidence overstates generality. Of only two real directed networks, ParPIC is slightly worse than S-PIC on Email-Eu (0.48 versus 0.49) and obtains 0.39±0.14 on PolBlogs. The largest gains occur on three synthetic models closely aligned with the proposed degree-balancing mechanism; no significance tests or broader modern baselines are provided.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported by one runtime plot without hardware, implementation details, error bars, or asymptotic analysis. With both probes and projection dimension set to √N, the advertised implementation can require O(t|E|√N) work and O(N^(3/2)) dense storage, and the unspecified “classical spectral clustering” comparison may not reflect sparse partial eigensolvers.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: the manuscript omits the k-NN preprocessing/scaling and explicit K choice, dataset sources, sink handling, random seeds, hardware, maximum diffusion horizon, KNEEDLE configuration and no-knee behavior, and several baseline implementation choices.

The assertion that the reversible operator “preserves directional dynamics” needs qualification: its effective conductance D_νP+P^T D_ν is symmetric and collapses each ordered pair into one symmetric weight. The paper does not characterize which directional structures remain distinguishable. Together with some contradictory definitions and very small appendix figures, this reduces both presentation precision and confidence in the central claims.

strengths: Presentation: The manuscript is polished, clearly organized, and supported by a useful pipeline diagram, algorithm, readable tables, and extensive appendices. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-odn07w42/call-1186df352d834a0fb732292432071112/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Technical merit: Combining a vertex-measure-dependent reversible operator with power-iteration clustering is simple and potentially useful for weakly connected directed graphs, assuming dangling vertices and periodicity are handled correctly.

Empirical scope: The evaluation includes ten K-NN datasets, synthetic directed block models, two real directed networks, ten baselines, repeated trials with standard deviations, and sensitivity analyses over diffusion time, projection dimension, and the vertex-measure parameter.

Significance: Eigen-free directed-graph clustering is practically relevant, and applying the same entropy selection and projection machinery to all PIC variants helps isolate differences among their operators.

Reproducibility and ethics: The paper provides code, dataset statistics, synthetic-model parameters, and substantial implementation discussion. No material ethical violation is evident from the benchmark-based experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. For the reversible, irreducible, aperiodic chain P=[[0.6,0.4],[0.1,0.9]] with stationary distribution (0.2,0.8), the paper's summed row entropy is 1.0957 at t=2 but decreases to 1.0746 at t=3. The proof misuses Jensen's inequality: its weights require column sums, whereas P is only row-stochastic. Moreover, because H is defined as a sum over N rows, its limit is N times the stationary-distribution entropy, not the single-row quantity shown in the proof. The resulting C(pi)-based bound in Proposition 3.6 is therefore also unsupported. This directly affects the claimed theoretical basis of the proposed time-selection mechanism.

Soundness: The practical embedding Z=P_(nu)^t Z0 approximately preserves ordinary Euclidean distances between rows of P_(nu)^t. The paper's diffusion distance instead weights coordinates by 1/pi_(nu), requiring projection of P_(nu)^t D_pi^(-1/2), or an equivalent covariance-weighted projection. Thus Algorithm 1 is not shown to approximate the diffusion geometry defined in Section 3.2. The JL claim also omits the necessary projection normalization and precise distribution.

Applicability: P=D_out^(-1)W is undefined at zero-outdegree sinks, yet the paper emphasizes that PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain many sinks without specifying a dangling-node convention. Weak connectivity also does not imply aperiodicity; a bipartite symmetrized support can make P_(nu) periodic, contradicting the broad convergence and applicability claims unless laziness or another correction is added.

Evidence and significance: The largest accuracy gains occur on constructed DiSBMs aligned with the proposed mechanism. On K-NN graphs ParPIC merely ties S-PIC in aggregate PRB, while evidence on naturally directed graphs is limited to two relatively small datasets. The PolBlogs AMI is only 0.39 despite being the best reported result. Broader comparisons with directed SBM inference, flow/community-detection methods, and modern scalable alternatives are needed.

Scalability evidence is insufficient: Figure 3 does not report hardware, software, sparse eigensolver, diffusion time, repetitions, uncertainty, or memory. With the default d=sqrt(N), ParPIC costs roughly O(t|E|sqrt(N)) and stores O(Nsqrt(N)) features, so superiority over computing only k eigenvectors with a modern sparse solver does not follow from the current comparison.

Originality: The reversible vertex-measure construction builds closely on Sevi et al., PIC is established, random projection is standard, and entropy-based scale selection is motivated by prior work. The integration is useful, but the manuscript does not sharply isolate a sufficiently strong new technical contribution—especially after the entropy theorem fails.

Presentation and reproducibility: The background incorrectly writes the generally nonsymmetric random-walk matrix as P=sum_i lambda_i phi_i phi_i^T. Important experimental details are also missing or ambiguous, including sink preprocessing, the gamma used in the main tables, feature scaling before K-NN construction, KNEEDLE settings and search horizon, projection variance/normalization, random seeds, eigensolver configuration, and runtime environment.

Limitations and ethics: There is no substantive limitations section, and the generic impact statement does not discuss failure on periodic or dangling-node graphs, sensitivity to gamma, the need to know k, or privacy considerations when inferring communities in communication networks. The ethical risk appears modest, but its treatment is cursory.

strengths: Soundness: For a valid row-stochastic P and positive ν, Eq. (3) has an appealing interpretation as a random walk on symmetric weights ν_iP_ij+ν_jP_ji; its reversibility and weak-connectivity-to-irreducibility properties are useful and mostly established clearly.

Significance: Combining this operator with power-iteration clustering, randomized embeddings, and automatic diffusion-time selection addresses a practically relevant directed-graph clustering problem without explicit eigendecomposition.

Evaluation: The study includes ten K-NN datasets, three directed SBMs, two real directed networks, ten baselines, repeated runs, and extensive sensitivity analyses for γ, t, projection dimension, and entropy probes. ParPIC is particularly strong on the tailored chain/core-periphery SBMs and improves substantially on PolBlogs.
Presentation: The main pipeline is easy to follow, with a useful overview figure, pseudocode, dataset statistics, baseline descriptions, and substantial appendices.

Reproducibility and ethics: The paper provides a public code URL and specifies the synthetic block matrices and many default parameters. This is a low-risk methodological contribution using standard benchmarks, with no apparent material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Proposition 3.5 is false. Its Jensen step treats P(k,j) as weights although they need not sum to one over k. A counterexample within the paper's own setting is the connected, aperiodic undirected graph with symmetric weights [[0,0,1],[0,0,1],[1,1,1]]. Its natural walk is recovered by P_(ν) when ν=π, yet the stated total row entropy decreases from approximately 2.881 at t=2 to 2.419 at t=3. Thus the claimed monotonic foundation for the elbow criterion does not hold.

Soundness: Proposition 3.6's variance bound relies on the resulting unsupported assertion H_i(t)≤C(π). There is also a normalization contradiction: Eq. (7) and the estimator define H as a sum over vertices, whereas the proof of Proposition 3.5 silently uses an average and gives the corresponding unscaled limit. The unbiased sampling identity survives, but the advertised bound does not follow as written.

Soundness and reproducibility: P=D_out^{-1}W requires every vertex to have positive out-degree, but the paper explicitly emphasizes that PolBlogs and Email-Eu contain sinks. No dangling-node convention or preprocessing is specified. With the usual zero-inverse convention P is not stochastic, invalidating the stochasticity proof and subsequent diffusion theory. Similarly, positive ν alone does not ensure aperiodicity, contrary to the discussion after Proposition 3.2.

Originality and claim scope: The manuscript attributes the parametrized reversible construction to closely related prior generalized-Laplacian work, while random projection is standard and related PIC machinery already exists. The genuinely new components and their distinction from Sevi et al. (2025) are not isolated sharply. Moreover, P_(ν) is itself a reversible walk on a symmetric weighted graph, so claims that it “preserves directional dynamics” require a formal account of which orientation information survives this weighted symmetrization.

Evidence: Real directed-network evidence consists of only two small graphs. On Email-Eu, ParPIC (0.48) is slightly below S-PIC (0.49), contradicting the claim of consistently outperforming all competitors; on PolBlogs its standard deviation is large (0.14), and no significance tests are reported. On K-NN graphs it ties S-PIC in aggregate PRB, so the main gains arise largely on synthetic models designed around the degree/flow effects the method targets.

Scalability and reproducibility: The runtime claim rests on one synthetic family and lacks hardware, implementation, repetition, uncertainty, memory, and asymptotic-cost details. Using d=√N can be expensive relative to modern sparse partial eigensolvers that compute only k eigenvectors. Other missing details include sink handling, feature scaling, the explicitly chosen K for K-NN graphs, degree normalization, random-projection scaling, k-means settings, and complete KNEEDLE search parameters.

Presentation and limitations: The background writes the generally nonsymmetric natural random walk as P=Σ_iλ_iφ_iφ_i^T, which is only valid after an appropriate symmetric transformation or in a weighted inner product. Several captions/text counts conflict, and the aperiodicity proof establishes only a self-loop sufficient condition. More importantly, there is no substantive limitations discussion covering failure on non-stochastic inputs, loss of nonreversible flow information, parameter sensitivity visible in Figure 11, or the narrow real-world evaluation. These unresolved central technical and evidential issues prevent acceptance despite the promising empirical idea.

Likewise, positive nu alone does not ensure aperiodicity; weakly connected bipartite graphs remain periodic unless the walk is made lazy.

Soundness and interpretation: The defined diffusion distance weights coordinates by 1/pi, but the implemented method clusters ordinary Euclidean rows of P_(nu)^t, and Z=P_(nu)^t Z_0 preserves those unweighted row distances. Without a D_pi^{-1/2} correction, this is not the claimed diffusion geometry except in special cases such as uniform pi.

Originality: P_(nu) is exactly a random walk on the symmetric conductance matrix D_nu P+P^T D_nu, closely derived from the cited generalized-Laplacian work; PIC and random projections are also established. The paper does not characterize what directional information survives this weighted symmetrization or provide cluster-recovery theory. With the entropy contribution theoretically invalid, the remaining novelty is modest.

Evidence: The strongest gains occur on hand-designed directed SBMs tailored to source-sink and degree-heterogeneity effects. On the ten K-NN graphs ParPIC only ties S-PIC in aggregate and is rarely best, while among the two real directed networks it loses slightly on Email-Eu and reaches only 0.39 AMI on PolBlogs. This is insufficient support for broad superiority claims, and small differences are not accompanied by significance tests.

Reproducibility and baseline validity: Critical choices are missing, including sink handling, feature scaling, an explicit K value for K-NN construction, dataset provenance/preprocessing, the entropy search horizon, KNEEDLE settings, k-means settings, hardware, and sparse eigensolver details. Appendix B also gives an apparently erroneous Simple-Herm definition: its reverse-edge case multiplies by W_ij while assuming W_ij=0, and the displayed normalization is not generally Hermitian. DSC+ handling for non-ergodic graphs is similarly ambiguous. These issues weaken confidence in the comparisons.

Scalability: No complete asymptotic analysis is supplied. With the defaults d=n=sqrt(N), embedding and entropy estimation can cost on the order of t|E|sqrt(N), which is not necessarily preferable to computing k eigenvectors when k is small. Figure 3 covers one synthetic family and omits hardware, solver configuration, memory, time-selection cost, and uncertainty, so it does not establish the broad scalability claim.

Limitations and ethics: There is no focused limitations discussion acknowledging the false monotonicity assumption, periodic graphs, sinks, known-k dependence, loss of nonreversible flow, or regimes where sqrt(N) projections are expensive. The generic impact statement also overlooks privacy and profiling concerns associated with clustering political and email networks and does not discuss their provenance or licensing.

strengths: Soundness (partial): when the natural walk P is well-defined and ν is strictly positive, Eq. 3 gives a simple stochastic, reversible operator with stationary measure proportional to ν+Pᵀν; weak connectivity also yields irreducible support.

Significance: scalable clustering for weakly connected directed graphs is important, and combining reversible diffusion, power iteration, sampled time selection, and random projection is potentially useful.

Evaluation: the paper compares against ten baselines, reports AMI over repeated runs, and includes extensive sensitivity studies for γ, diffusion time, embedding dimension, degree heterogeneity, and cluster count.
Presentation: the pipeline and algorithm are easy to follow, the manuscript is visually polished, and the appendix provides proofs, dataset statistics, and baseline descriptions.

Reproducibility and limitations: a public code link and practical defaults are provided. The paper also candidly observes that directionality offers little benefit on reciprocal K-NN graphs and that γ can be dataset-dependent. No acute ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 3.5 is false. Its Jensen step treats {P(k,j)} over k as convex weights, although a row-stochastic P need not have columns summing to one. For the reversible ergodic matrix [[0.1,0.9],[0.2,0.8]], global row entropy is approximately 0.8255, 0.9576, and 0.9473 at times 1, 2, and 3, contradicting monotonicity. The proof also switches from the sum in Eq. 7 to an average and omits a factor N in the limit. Consequently, the bound H_i(t)≤C(π) used in Proposition 3.6, and hence its variance and concentration claims, are unsupported. This directly weakens the theoretical basis of the proposed automatic time selection.

Scope: P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet the paper specifically highlights sinks in PolBlogs and Email-Eu without stating a dangling-node convention or preprocessing rule. Moreover, weak connectivity and positive ν do not ensure aperiodicity, contrary to the prose after Proposition 3.2; a bipartite support can remain periodic, invalidating convergence claims on the advertised graph class.

Methodological mismatch: Eq. 4 defines diffusion distance using the 1/π-weighted norm, whereas Z=P_(ν)^t Z(0) is justified by Johnson-Lindenstrauss preservation of unweighted Euclidean distances between rows of P_(ν)^t. Without applying D_π^{-1/2}, the embedding actually clustered by Algorithm 1 is not an approximation to the stated diffusion geometry.

The claim of preserving directional dynamics is insufficiently formalized. D_νP+PᵀD_ν is a symmetric affinity that creates reverse transitions; direction can affect its weights, but the manuscript does not characterize what directional information survives this reversibilization.

Evidence: the strongest gains occur on synthetic core-periphery and chain SBMs designed around asymmetric flow. There are only two small intrinsically directed real datasets; on Email-Eu, ParPIC scores 0.48 versus 0.49 for S-PIC, contradicting the claim that it consistently outperforms competitors. On K-NN graphs it merely ties S-PIC in aggregate PRB. The rounded PRB of 1.00 obscures the Email-Eu loss.

Scalability is not convincingly established. There is no complexity analysis for the √N-dimensional projection and √N-probe entropy computation, which requires repeated operations on an n-by-N state matrix. Figure 3 compares only against an unspecified “classical spectral clustering” implementation on one synthetic family, without hardware, solver, timing protocol, variability, or a modern sparse eigensolver comparison.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: the manuscript omits K and feature preprocessing for K-NN graphs, sink handling, entropy search horizon and KNEEDLE settings, exact random-projection normalization, k-means restart details, and what varies across the reported runs. DiSBM-CP is also inconsistently described as having 4000 vertices versus 3×1300=3900.

Originality and limitations: the reversible operator is closely built on Sevi et al. (2025), while PIC and random projections are established; the main claimed new theoretical element, entropy-based selection, is unsound. The limitations discussion does not acknowledge the invalid graph-domain assumptions, limited real-network evidence, or possible privacy and profiling concerns when clustering social and email networks; the impact statement is boilerplate.

strengths: The parametrized reversible operator is a coherent way to apply power-iteration clustering to directed graphs; its reversibility and irreducibility properties are useful when the natural walk and positive vertex measure are well-defined.

The empirical study is broad for this niche, covering 10 baselines, synthetic and real graphs, 100-run summaries, runtime experiments, and extensive sensitivity analyses. ParPIC is particularly promising on the directed SBM and PolBlogs experiments.
Presentation is polished and generally clear. The pipeline, algorithm, tables, figures, synthetic-model parameters, and appendices make the main ideas easy to follow.
The paper provides a public code link and uses standard public datasets. The work presents no evident material ethical concern, although the impact discussion is minimal.
weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 3.5, which motivates the entropy-based time selector, is false. For example, the irreducible, aperiodic, reversible chain P=[[0.999,0.001],[0.785,0.215]] has summed row entropy H(1) approximately 0.5284 but H(2) approximately 0.1990. The proof incorrectly applies Jensen using P(k,j) as weights over k even though those weights need not sum to one unless P is doubly stochastic.

The entropy analysis is internally inconsistent: Eq. 7 defines H as a sum, the proof switches to an average, and the claimed limit omits the resulting factor of N. Consequently, the range argument used in Proposition 3.6 is invalid, although its basic unbiasedness result remains true. Moreover, monotonicity and convergence alone would not establish that a curve elbow identifies the best clustering scale.

The practical embedding is not justified by the stated diffusion geometry. Equation 4 uses distances weighted by 1/pi, whereas Z=P^t Z0 preserves unweighted Euclidean distances between rows of P^t. A diffusion-distance-preserving projection would require the corresponding stationary-measure weighting. This discrepancy is especially important in the degree-heterogeneous regime emphasized by the paper.

The advertised domain is not supported as written. P=D_out^{-1}W is undefined at sinks, yet the paper explicitly says its real graphs contain many sinks and gives no dangling-node convention. Weak connectivity also does not ensure aperiodicity, so P^t need not converge on bipartite support; no lazy-walk correction is specified.

Significance is overstated by the evidence. On the ten K-NN datasets ParPIC merely ties S-PIC in aggregate, and on Email-Eu it scores 0.48 versus S-PIC's 0.49. The largest gains occur on synthetic structures tailored to asymmetric degree/flow patterns, while only two intrinsically directed real networks are tested and no significance tests are reported. Thus the claim of consistently outperforming all competitors is inaccurate.

The scalability claim is insufficiently substantiated. Both the embedding and sampled entropy computation use about sqrt(N) dense probes, giving costs on the order of t|E|sqrt(N) and substantial memory; this is not compared carefully with sparse partial eigensolvers. Figure 3 omits hardware, solver configuration, repeated-run uncertainty, and detailed graph-density information.

Reproducibility has important gaps despite the code link: K-NN preprocessing and K, sink handling, projection distribution and normalization, KNEEDLE horizon/settings, and clustering/eigensolver configurations are underspecified. DiSBM-CP is listed as 4000 vertices despite using three groups of 1300. The written Simple-Herm definition also multiplies by W_ij in a case requiring W_ij=0 and gives a normalization that is generally not Hermitian, casting doubt on baseline fidelity.

Originality is modest once the invalid entropy contribution is discounted: the vertex-measure operator substantially builds on Sevi et al. (2025), while PIC and random projection are established techniques. The manuscript also lacks a substantive limitations discussion covering these applicability, complexity, and evaluation restrictions. These central technical and evidential issues prevent acceptance in the current form.
